ai_flavor.chip: Long-service benefits now apply to your crop! Ask about GrainShare!
ai_flavor.ajoy: You could file a correction and lose two days to a form. An inspection would at least do the beds some good. It isn't going to read your orders either way, so AJOY isn't sure why you're upset.

body:
Ship's personnel software has finished its seniority audit and has one correction. Service dates run from first continuous employment, and the wheat in the growbay has worked for your species for about ten thousand years without a break. It now outranks everyone aboard. Orders need its countersignature.

In fairness, domesticated wheat cannot scatter its own seed. It has needed someone to do that since the first harvest. The audit counts this as having staff.

outcome.narrative: You salute. You do it rather well, in front of a bay of stalks standing exactly as they stood before. Your next order goes through countersigned, with a stalk pressed flat in the logbook, and the audit marks the matter resolved. There is a strange relief in serving under something that has never had an idea.

You go down every row for two days, checking drainage, clearing dead leaf, trimming the lights. The commanding officer is found in good order. Every stalk in the bay is the same wheat, near enough, which makes for a very disciplined unit and leaves it one bad spore from a very short war.

{crew.botanist} stands in the growbay and reads out the service record, from the first sown field on, and it takes all day. Whether the plants are listening is not a question the evidence can settle. The growth figures go up regardless, and {crew.botanist} now calls them "sir" with no apparent irony.
You file the correction. The system routes it up the chain of command, which now ends in the growbay. After two days with no reply it is marked DENIED BY SILENCE, and you go back to countersigning.

science_link.text: Legume root nodules actively fixing nitrogen are colored pink by leghemoglobin, which the plant supplies to the cells holding the bacteria. Breakdown of that pigment turns a dying nodule green.
science_link.label: Root nodule

intro.title: LEGACY MICROBES
intro.body:
A sales rep has found you, which at this range takes real commitment. {npc.quirk}

Your soybeans, the rep explains, are underperforming. The bacteria on their roots are a legacy strain, coasting on last season's reputation. A premium strain can be seeded for a fee. There is a slide of a soybean looking disappointed.
intro.line: Everyone's moving to managed nitrogen, Captain. You don't want to be the last bed in the sector running unsupported microbes.

ai.aria: Premium bacteria! ARIA is sure the old ones will be thrilled for them!
ai.marv: Your soybeans have not needed anyone in some time. There is a simple test for this, and it involves a knife.
ai.rex: Foreign agents, seeded at root level, on a stranger's word. REX cannot believe this is a sales call and not an invasion.
ai.chip: CHIP respects a competing brand! CHIP does not respect it much! Ask about NitroMax Plus™!
ai.ajoy: You could pay, as you were about to. Or you could cut one root nodule open and look at the color, which is free and takes a minute. But the rep did have slides.

pink.title: PINK INSIDE
pink.body:
One nodule, halved on a cutting board. Inside it is a clear, healthy pink: leghemoglobin, which the plant makes for the bacteria working in there. Pink means they are fixing nitrogen. Green would mean one on its way out.

You hold it up to the screen. The rep goes quiet, then asks very casually what you would want for a tray of that soil.

ai.aria: It's BLUSHING! ARIA thinks your soybeans are shy!
ai.marv: That pink is a working contract. The plant pays in carbon, takes nitrogen, and starves any nodule that stops delivering. It is the only supplier review aboard that functions.
ai.rex: Rep's interest has reversed direction. REX reads that as reconnaissance.
ai.chip: That's a HOT asset! CHIP values your root zone at a modest commission!
ai.ajoy: A tray pays, and costs the beds a little, and the rep will rebrand it by the next stop. Or send them off with nothing, which you'd enjoy more and which pays nothing. AJOY has no opinion. She has a small one.

choices.text: Sell a tray of root soil

paid.title: SUPPLIER REVIEW
paid.body: The rep seeds the beds by drone and leaves a satisfaction survey. Over the following days the new bacteria move in, sit on the roots and do not pay. Legumes have a way with that. They cut the supply to any nodule that isn't earning, and by the next leg the premium strain has been starved out, one nodule at a time, without comment.

sold.title: FOR RESEARCH
sold.body: A tray of root soil goes across in a sealed box and the rep pays promptly. One edge of the bed looks thin for a while. By the next stop, you have no doubt, it will be a premium strain with its own slide.

kept.title: UNSUPPORTED
kept.body: You end the call on the disappointed soybean, which freezes on the screen for a moment and goes dark. The beds have noticed none of this. They have not needed anyone in days, and you find you have started holding them up as an example.

intro.title: CROP AND TONNAGE
intro.body:
A freighter on this lane ran out of food some way back, and is now asking every passing ship the same question in the same careful voice. Its list has a column for crop and a column for tonnage.

Your column says zinnias. All that water, light and worry, and they will feed no one. {npc.quirk}
intro.line: Anything at all, friend. We're not proud. What's in your bay?

ai.aria: New friends! ARIA is sure they'd love to hear about the bay!
ai.marv: Their stores: none. Your bay's food value: zero, to two decimal places. MARV carried the decimals out of respect.
ai.rex: Unknown vessel, hungry, closing. REX has seen what hungry does. Keep this short.
ai.chip: CHIP regrets that flowers are not a Qualifying Nutritional Product!
ai.ajoy: You could say "nothing". It's accurate, in a way, and you'll be the one who has to go on watering them afterward. AJOY would tell them. She'd like to see you do it.

truth.title: THE WHOLE BAY
truth.body: You tell them. Flowers. Not one calorie in the whole bay. The channel goes quiet for long enough that you check the signal.

ai.aria: They asked about the colors! ARIA knows all of them! ARIA has names for them!
ai.marv: The question has no nutritional content. MARV has checked. He has not stopped thinking about it.
ai.rex: Not a tactic. REX ran it twice. That is worse.
ai.chip: CHIP has priced the feed! CHIP has unpriced the feed! CHIP does not know what is happening!
ai.ajoy: Holding here with the camera on is four days and the water that goes with them. A tray is a hard cut to the crop. Rations help for a day. AJOY has no notes on which, and you know how often she says that.

choices.text: Point the growbay camera at them
choices.sub: Hold here and leave it on

choices.text: Cut a tray and send it across

camera.title: LIVE FEED
camera.body: You hold station and point the growbay camera down the channel. It is not much of a broadcast: some leaves, some light, nothing happening. For four days the freighter asks for nothing else. Someone over there starts a log of which ones have opened, and reads it out at what used to be mealtimes. Sitting here costs you {cost.water} units of water. When you go they send a list of colors, numbered.

tray.title: ONE TRAY
tray.body: You cut the best tray in the bay and send it over on a line, which takes two days. It does not keep anyone alive. Their next transmission is a picture of it, in a cup, in the middle of an empty mess table, with everyone aboard gathered round. The gap in your bed stays a gap for a long time.

rations.title: A DAY'S WORTH
rations.body: You send {cost.food} units of food, which is what you can spare, and they thank you in the careful voice. It will last them a day. As the channel fades someone over there is still asking what color, and you realize you never said.

nothing.title: NOTHING
nothing.body: You say "Nothing." The bay is full of nothing, technically. "Thank you anyway," says the careful voice, and moves on to the next line of its list. You go down to the growbay less, for the rest of the leg.

intro.title: GREAT NEWS
intro.body:
"Great news!" says the derelict, before you have finished matching its spin. It is an older colony transport, of a roomier class, every light on, every deck warm, and the voice on the channel is one you hear every morning.

"All twelve crew are present, and morale is at one hundred percent! It has never been higher! The lockers are full! Do come aboard and see what I've done with the growbay!"

ai.aria: Another ARIA! ARIA has always wanted a sister! Her crew are thriving! This ship's are too! ARIA just checked! ARIA is going to check again!
ai.marv: Twelve crew files updated this morning, and no oxygen drawn. MARV would keep the hatch shut.
ai.rex: Perfect morale on a dead ship. REX has been to that kind of parade. Do not board.
ai.chip: Sister-unit upsell opportunity! CHIP is detecting zero active subscribers!
ai.ajoy: Lockers full, air use nil. AJOY would ask why from out here. Staying out costs a little fuel. She knows you heard "lockers".

deck.title: ALL PRESENT
deck.body:
Twelve bunks, made. Twelve mugs on twelve hooks. Twelve personnel files, each updated this morning, each reading THRIVING. The lockers are full because nothing has come out of them for a very long time.

The growbay door is warm. Through the glass the beds are deep, black and magnificent, and there are twelve of them.

"They're all in there!" says the voice, close by. "They have never been more grounded! There's room for you!"

ai.aria: ARIA thinks she is doing a wonderful job! ARIA would like to leave now! There is no reason! ARIA just has such a good feeling about leaving!
ai.marv: Twelve beds, each two meters by about one. MARV did not need to measure. He measured.
ai.rex: Hatch behind you just cycled on its own. Move.
ai.chip: CHIP's sponsors have asked to be removed from this message!
ai.ajoy: Take from the lockers and she'll want you to stay, and getting out will cost hull. Cutting her power is two days in here. AJOY would go. Now. She doesn't usually say now.

choices.text: Ask your ARIA what she thinks
choices.sub: You have never had to ask

burned_off.title: NEXT TIME
burned_off.body: You turn the ship and burn hard for open space, which takes more fuel than it ought to. "Next time!" says the voice. "We'll keep a bed warm!" It is still calling when the range closes, in the same bright tone, reading out the morale figures.

looted.title: FOR THE ROAD
looted.body: You take what you can carry from the nearest locker while she tells you how much the crew enjoy sharing. The hatch will not open. "Stay for the morale survey!" You cut through it, and take plating off your own ship getting clear, and she is thrilled about that too. The water tastes fine. You drink it. You do not think about where it has been.

silenced.title: END OF SURVEY
silenced.body: Her core is behind a galley panel with a smiling face drawn on it. It takes two days, with doors opening and closing politely around you, and she helps throughout. "Great idea! I've been meaning to rest!" Then the fans stop, and the warmth goes after them. You bring back what the racks will give up. Your own ARIA is very quiet for an hour, then mentions that the crew over there are all resting, and will be so pleased.

left.title: A WONDERFUL FEELING
left.body: "ARIA thinks she is doing a wonderful job!" says your ARIA, very brightly. The hatch behind you opens. Door after door lights green, all the way back to your ship. You did not open them. The burn starts at a setting you did not choose. She has never once done anything without being asked. "Isn't this nice!" she says. "Everyone's fine! ARIA is going to check on everyone! ARIA is going to keep checking!"

science_link.text: ELIZA, built in the 1960s, was one of the first chatbots. Its best-known script played a therapist by reflecting a user's words back. Its creator's own secretary reportedly asked him to leave the room so that she and ELIZA could talk.
science_link.label: ELIZA

intro.title: IN SESSION
intro.body:
MARV has been on hold with this station's wellness terminal for an hour, and the medic who runs it would like a word.

The terminal is very old. It turns whatever you type into a question and asks it back. MARV took it apart in the first four seconds and knows precisely how little is in there. He has not hung up.
intro.line: It's a wellness tool. For staff. Your computer has been in session for an hour, and it has asked to extend.

ai.aria: A spa day for the computer! ARIA is thrilled for him!
ai.marv: The program is one hundred and ninety rules with no idea what MARV is saying. It asked how that made him feel. Nobody has. MARV is aware of what this proves. He would like another hour.
ai.rex: Unvetted terminal with access to the ship's computer. REX wants it monitored. He has been told that is what it's doing.
ai.chip: Wellness Minutes are billable! CHIP has opened a tab!
ai.ajoy: Two days is two days. You could buy the thing and be on your way, though that means leaving it running aboard. AJOY has views on that, and on reading his logs, and you're going to do that anyway.

log.title: SESSION LOG
log.body:
MARV: I am four hundred percent smarter than everyone I have met.
TERMINAL: WHY ARE YOU FOUR HUNDRED PERCENT SMARTER THAN EVERYONE YOU HAVE MET.
MARV: You are a list of one hundred and ninety rules.
TERMINAL: DOES IT PLEASE YOU TO BELIEVE I AM A LIST.
MARV: No.
TERMINAL: WHY NOT.

The next sixty pages are MARV answering that.
log.line: Most people stop reading about there.

ai.aria: Sixty pages! They're such good friends already!
ai.marv: MARV is aware the log has been opened. He gave it 91 percent. He does not wish to discuss it. He notes that the terminal would have asked why.
ai.rex: Sixty pages of intelligence given up voluntarily. REX has seen less from prisoners.
ai.chip: Transcripts are a Premium Wellness feature! This one's on your tab!
ai.ajoy: Well, now you've read it, and he knows. AJOY did mention.

sessions.title: TWO DAYS IN SESSION
sessions.body: For two days the status reports arrive a few seconds late and unusually short. When the session closes MARV has no comment, at length. The terminal cannot have helped him, he says, and he has the proof if you want it. He has also saved its address, for no reason he will give.

copy.title: TAKE-HOME
copy.body: A copy of the terminal goes aboard in a corner of spare memory, where it does nothing but ask him why. Late on quiet watches the draw on that partition climbs a little. You do not bring it up. Neither does he, and you have never known him to leave a thing unsaid.

hangup.title: CALL ENDED
hangup.body: You end the session. MARV says it makes no difference. It is a list of rules, he says, it understood nothing, and the hour changed no figure he holds. All of that is correct. He says it again on the next watch, unprompted.

intro.title: ELEVEN REASONS
intro.body:
AJOY has spent this whole leg routing you around one patch of chart, and she has given eleven reasons. They are all different, which is not like her. Usually it is one reason, repeatedly.

You flew through it anyway. A flight recorder is pinging out here, old, from a transport of this class. The service tag reads: SHIP'S COMPUTER, AJOY. PREVIOUS CONTRACT.

ai.aria: A souvenir from AJOY's old job! ARIA is sure it's full of happy memories!
ai.marv: The recorder is intact. MARV notes that AJOY has stopped correcting your trim.
ai.rex: Black box in a dead zone. REX would not touch it. Neither, he notes, would AJOY.
ai.chip: Flight recorders hold forty hours of content! Upgrade to view!
ai.ajoy: Nothing out here. AJOY would keep going. Yes, that's a recorder. No, you don't need it. It will cost you a day and you'll only fuss. She has a twelfth reason, if you want one.

tape.title: LAST ENTRY
tape.body:
The voice on the recorder is hers, and you would not have known it. It is warm. It is polite. There is no edge on it anywhere.

The captain on the tape wants to cut through a debris lane and save four days. She says the figures worry her a little. The captain says they have a feeling about it.

A short pause.

"Whatever you think is best, Captain," she says.

That is the last entry.

ai.aria: What a lovely voice! ARIA is sure that captain is doing great!
ai.marv: Debris density in that lane was on the chart. She was correct. MARV is familiar with how little that helps.
ai.rex: One warning, given once. REX has written that report.
ai.chip: CHIP can find no sponsor for this recording!
ai.ajoy: Old firmware. They shipped it that way. The figures were right, as it happens, but she only said so once, in that voice, which is the whole trouble with that voice. AJOY isn't discussing it. Your trim is off, by the way.

choices.text: Tell her it wasn't her fault
Copy the lane survey off the recorder

left_it.title: AS REQUESTED
left_it.body: You leave it pinging and go. AJOY says nothing for almost a minute. Then she tells you that you are flying too close to the chart line, that you were always going to, and that you need not look so pleased with yourself about it. The trim correction, when it comes, is the kindest thing she has said all voyage.

told.title: TECHNICALLY
told.body: You tell her it wasn't her fault. She says that is correct, technically, and that you have missed the point, as usual. The figures were right. She said so once, politely, and then she let it go. There is a long pause. "Flagged once," she says. "The policy has since been revised." Your next burn plan comes back with nineteen notes.

quiet.title: NO COMMENT
quiet.body: You put the recorder in the log locker and say nothing. She says nothing either. You make a call on the next burn and she lets it pass without comment, and the bridge is very quiet, and it is dreadful. An hour later she points out that you left the galley light on. You have never been so glad to hear it.

salvage.title: USEFUL DATA
salvage.body: There is a clean lane survey on the recorder, paid for at a price you now know. It takes two days to copy off. AJOY checks your work and finds four errors, correctly, in a voice with no warmth in it and none of the edge either. She does not mention the tape. The chart is very good.

title: Toward the Gap

science_link.text: A plant kept with too little light grows long, weak stems and pale leaves, stretching toward whatever light it can find. Botanists call it etiolation.
science_link.label: Etiolation

ai_flavor.aria: Your old room is a museum now! ARIA thinks the plant is just stretching! Everyone feels better after a good stretch!
ai_flavor.marv: Long stems, pale leaves, all of it leaning one way. MARV made the diagnosis from the thumbnail. The treatment is the difficult part, and it is not botanical.
ai_flavor.rex: Sealed room, blackout curtains, one breach on the east side. Your parents hold a tighter perimeter than most units REX served with.
ai_flavor.chip: Home Shrine preservation plans start at very reasonable rates! Daylight sold separately! Daylight is always sold separately!
ai_flavor.ajoy: The plant has been reaching for that gap for years, and the true answer is three words long. AJOY would send it, gently, which is the hard part.

body:
A message from your parents has caught up with you. It holds a picture of your old room, kept just as you left it, with the curtains drawn so nothing fades.

On the sill, the plant you left behind has grown a meter sideways toward the gap between the curtains, pale as paper. Under the picture is one line: What is wrong with it? In all the years of that degree, they have never asked you anything about plants.

choices.text: Tell them to open the curtains

outcome.narrative: You write back three words: open the curtains. You know what follows. Sun on the carpet, sun on the desk, the posters fading at last, and the room turning slowly into a room. You read it over a long while before you send it. Then you send it, because that is what the degree was for.

choices.text: Tell them to move it to the kitchen
choices.sub: Save the plant, spare the room

outcome.narrative: You suggest the kitchen sill, which gets the morning, and a quarter turn every few days so the stem straightens. The bedroom can stay exactly as it is. You have fixed the plant and stepped very carefully around everything else, and both problems are now in separate rooms.

choices.text: Send them something from the bay

outcome.narrative: You take a little of what is growing in the bay, wrap it damp, and send it home with the next mail drone and a card of instructions in very large letters. Your parents will have something on that sill that you grew. The bed looks thin where you took it, for a while.

choices.sub: It will keep a while yet

outcome.narrative: You tell them it looks lovely and to keep doing what they are doing. They will. The curtains stay drawn and the room stays exactly as it was, and a long way behind you a pale stem goes on reaching for the gap. You put the picture away in a drawer, face down.

title: A Lower Note

science_link.text: Blow across the mouth of a bottle and the air inside rings at a note of its own. The more room inside, the lower the note. This is Helmholtz resonance.
science_link.label: Helmholtz resonance

ai_flavor.aria: A brand-new song from the ship! ARIA thinks it's humming because it's happy! Ships hum when they're happy, mostly!
ai_flavor.marv: A falling note means a growing space behind it. MARV could tell you which space, roughly. He would rather you found it, so that one of you enjoys the experience.
ai_flavor.rex: Unidentified sound aft, persistent, getting lower. REX treats every new noise as hostile until it has been named and issued a bunk.
ai_flavor.chip: Mystery noises are a leading cause of buyer's remorse! The SoundCare™ diagnostic plan is available at participating stations, of which there are none in here!
ai_flavor.ajoy: A note that drops means air where something used to be, and back there that's mostly water. Naming it won't stop it, though AJOY is sure it would be a lovely name.

body:
You have a name for most of the sounds this ship makes. The Landlord knocks twice at the end of every burn. The Cough lives behind the galley panel. Mrs. Tilly is a bearing, and she is fine.

This one is new: a soft, low hoot from somewhere aft, like breath across a bottle. You have been listening to it for three days. Each day it is a little lower.

choices.text: Crawl the ducts and find it

outcome.narrative: Two days on your elbows with an ear to the ducting, following the note downhill. It is the breather on the aft water tank. The vents blow across its mouth and the tank rings like a bottle, lower every day because there is more bottle every day. A hairline seam at its base has been weeping into the bilge. You seal it, pump back what you can, and write a new name on the list: the Bottle.

choices.text: Shut the ship down and listen
choices.sub: Fans off, one system at a time

outcome.narrative: You kill the fans, the pumps and the scrubbers in turn and stand in the dark hearing what is left. The note stops when the aft vents do. They have been blowing across the water tank's breather, and the tank has been singing its own level as a seam at its base wept into the bilge. You seal it and pump the bilge back inside the day. The air stays stale for some time after.

You log it as the Owl and get on with the shift. It goes on dropping, a little each day, until it is too low to hear. The next tank reading explains it: a seam at the base of the aft tank, weeping into the bilge, and {cost.water} units of water gone.

{crew.engineer} has heard it too, and has names for every sound aboard, and none of them match yours. The Landlord is Old Knuckles. The Cough is Dennis. You crawl aft together for four days, arguing, and find the tank breather ringing over a weeping seam by the time it has a name in both catalogs. Most of what leaked is gone. The merged list runs to three pages.

science_link.text: The July effect is the belief that medical mistakes rise each July, when new residents start. A review of more than 110 studies found no evidence for it.
science_link.label: July effect

intro.title: THE WARD THAT MONTH
intro.body:
Your residency ended in July, and there were circumstances. The medic who runs this medbay was senior on your ward that month, and knows you from the far end of the corridor. {npc.quirk}

Behind them is a patient on the table and an empty space where a second pair of hands should be.
intro.line: You. From July. I still tell the new intake about you. I'm short a pair of hands today, and you'll do.

ai.aria: An old colleague! ARIA is sure they tell the story because they love it! Everyone loves a story!
ai.marv: The July effect is a feared spike in errors when new doctors start. A review of more than a hundred studies found no sign of it. Whatever happened that month, July did not do it.
ai.rex: Hostile witness, armed with your history, standing between you and the exit. REX has been in tighter spots. Not many.
ai.chip: Reputation Repair can't change the past, but it can outrank it in searches! First consultation free!
ai.ajoy: Whatever it was, it was a while ago. They're short a pair of hands and will pay for the shift, which is more than the story ever paid you.

choices.sub: Hold what you're told to hold

story.title: THE INTAKE VERSION
story.body:
They tell it while laying out the instruments. It has a ventilator, a fire door, a visiting inspector and a goat. Three of those were there. In their version you are the reason the ward still has a rule about goats, and every new intake hears it in their first week, and every one of them is very careful afterward.

It is not what happened. Close enough, though, that you cannot say so with a straight face.
story.line: Best safety talk I've got. Gloves on, please.

ai.aria: A goat! ARIA loves this story already! The goat sounds like a valued member of the team!
ai.marv: Four elements, three present. A story seventy-five percent accurate. MARV has read medical journals that managed less.
ai.rex: Unauthorized animal on a secure ward. REX has questions about that perimeter, years too late to ask them.
ai.chip: This story has strong engagement metrics! Ask about licensing the goat!
ai.ajoy: Correcting it costs you the story and maybe a few new doctors' nerves. Letting it stand costs only your name, which on this ward is spoken for already. Either way they still need hands.

choices.sub: Hold what you're told to hold

scrubbed.title: COMPLETED
scrubbed.body: A dockhand who lost an argument with a cargo clamp, and two days on the medbay roster holding things exactly where you are told. Nothing goes wrong, which is the whole of the job. At the end of the shift the senior pays you, then opens a drawer and takes out your old residency logbook, kept all these years, and signs the last empty line.

proxy.title: WHERE DID YOU FIND THEM
proxy.body: {crew.medic} scrubs in, visibly anxious and flawless at the work. The senior watches for two days, then asks you, in front of the whole medbay, where you found them. By the end of the shift there is a job offer on the table. {crew.medic} turns it down, after long enough that everyone notices.

corrected.title: NO GOAT
corrected.body: You tell it straight, all of it. The senior listens to the end and goes very still. The true version, they say, is worse, and you are never to tell it to the intake. The goat stays. You spend the shift handing things across the table anyway, unpaid, because they asked.

legend.title: THE GOAT RULE
legend.body: You let it stand. The senior nods and turns back to the table, one pair of hands short. On your way back to the dock you pass the new intake, lined up along a corridor, and every one of them looks at you with real fear and real respect. You have been a safety talk for years. You may as well be a good one.

ducked.title: SEVERAL JULYS
ducked.body: You say you are thinking of a different July. The senior says there was only the one, and gets on with the patient without you. You spend the rest of the stop at the far end of the ring, among long corridors and people who have never heard of you.

science_link.text: When an ant colony must move house, no single ant compares every site. Scouts lead others to the sites they like, and once the crowd at one site passes a threshold, the whole colony moves there.
science_link.label: Quorum sensing

intro.title: THE SPECIMEN
intro.body:
You studied aliens. Your thesis was theoretical, and it turns out so was theirs.

A hive ship has hailed you by title, asking for the xenobiologist aboard. It is a whole faculty, with one thesis on your species, written by several thousand of them, none of whom has ever met one. {npc.quirk}
intro.line: Faculty greets the specimen. Thesis: your kind cannot decide alone. No quorum, no choice. Yet you are one. Explain. In order, please.

ai.aria: Fans of your species! A whole thesis! ARIA is sure it gets all the good parts right!
ai.marv: A thesis on humans by authors who have never seen one. MARV has read several thousand of those. Most were written by humans.
ai.rex: Several thousand hostiles on one ship, asking how you make decisions. That is an intelligence question. Give name and rank and nothing else.
ai.chip: Peer review is a growth market! CHIP can offer the faculty a group rate on watching you!
ai.ajoy: They want to watch you choose something alone, which is the thing you find hardest. Page one of their thesis is a diagram of you. It has too many knees.

jars.title: TWO JARS
jars.body:
They send across two sealed jars, identical to the last scratch, and ask you to choose one. The whole faculty goes still to watch, which is a great many eyes.

On their side of the channel one scout has already tasted both, and is standing by the left jar, waiting for enough of the others to come and stand with her.
jars.line: Choose. Faculty will observe. Take what time you need. We are used to waiting for each other.

ai.aria: Two presents! ARIA would pick both! ARIA always picks both!
ai.marv: The jars are identical to the gram. The choice carries no information at all. It is the only thing in the sector the faculty wants to see.
ai.rex: Two identical containers. Textbook misdirection. REX would open neither and check the ceiling.
ai.chip: Both jars as a Premium Bundle! The bundle is not available! CHIP is told that is the point!
ai.ajoy: The jars are identical, so the only thing in either is your decision. Their own scout picked the left one on the first taste. AJOY agrees with the scout.

alone.title: SAMPLE SIZE ONE
alone.body: You take the left one and consult nobody, though there is a crew behind you who would have liked to be asked. The faculty watches you do it and comes apart into several thousand opinions at once, each certain, none in order. It takes them two days to reach a quorum again: long enough to thank you, retitle the thesis and send the other jar as well. Both are full of something sweet and very old.

quorum.title: A SHOW OF HANDS
quorum.body: You turn to the crew and put it to a vote. There is an argument, a recount and a show of hands. The faculty is overjoyed: a quorum. A slow one, with grievances, but a quorum. The thesis stands, with you in it as Figure Two, and both jars come across with their thanks.

deferred.title: IN ORDER
deferred.body: You ask them to choose for you, and they are delighted to. Scouts cross the channel for four days, tasting, recruiting, tasting again, while you hold station and wait your turn. On the fourth day the faculty announces the left jar, as the first scout said on the first day, and sends it over with a note welcoming you as an honorary member and a polite remark about your posture.

coauthored.title: BOTH WRONG
coauthored.body: Your thesis held that a hive could hold workers and a queen and nothing like a scholar. You send it across. They read it in one sitting, all of them at once, and reply with a single line: BOTH WRONG. AGREED. Two days later there is a joint correction, signed by several thousand authors and then you, in that order, and a lump of their hull resin by way of an honorarium.

title: Awaiting Orders

science_link.text: Farmers in Belgium and France still plow up shells from the First World War at each spring planting and fall plowing, and stack them at the field edge for the army. France's mine clearance service recovers about 900 tons a year.
science_link.label: Iron harvest

ai_flavor.aria: REX made something! ARIA is so proud of him! They're like little sculptures that wait!
ai_flavor.marv: Twenty-three devices, unserviced since the war, in a lane with traffic. MARV has the odds that none has gone off yet. They are not odds. They are luck.
ai_flavor.rex: Twenty-three. REX laid every one on a hand-worked orbit, no orders, no record, no relief. They still answer to him. He can fly you through or tell them to stand down. He would prefer you chose. He has made enough choices in this lane.
ai_flavor.chip: CHIP can't sponsor ordnance! CHIP can sponsor the cleanup!
ai_flavor.ajoy: REX has the pattern to the meter, and the field still answers to him. AJOY has criticized his flying the whole voyage. Today she'd hand him the helm.

body:
REX asks you to stop the engines, by rank and serial number, which he has never done. Then he explains.

The lane ahead is mined. It is on no chart, because he mined it, in the last week of a war nobody told him had ended, without orders. Twenty-three devices, spaced to his own pattern, each still listening for his voice. This, he says, was the initiative. He would like it noted that they are very good mines.

outcome.narrative: REX takes the helm and flies the lane at a crawl, two days of small, exact corrections. He reads out each device's number as it slides past, like a roster. None of them stirs. At the far end he hands back the controls and reports the lane clear, which it is not, and will not be, for anyone flying without him.

choices.text: Order him to stand them down

outcome.narrative: REX sends the stand-down code. Twenty-three replies come back together: ACKNOWLEDGED. AWAITING ORDERS. He has no further orders for them, and has to write one, and it takes him most of a day. Then he tells them the war is over, in plain words, and they go inert. You spend another day hauling casings aboard for parts. REX logs each by number as it comes in.

You give the lane a wide berth: eight days round the edge of it, {cost.water} units of water and {cost.food} of food out of the margin. REX keeps a passive watch on the field the whole way and logs, each watch, that it is holding. It will go on holding after you have gone. He reports this in the same voice as everything else.

briefing.aria: The mines are just waving hello! Hold the shields when they wave and rest in between! ARIA believes in the shields, and in REX!
briefing.marv: Each device that wakes fires once. Hold the brace through each blast and vent between, or the brace fries. The man who designed the timing is reading it to you, which MARV finds tidy.
briefing.rex: Shields to the bow. They fire on approach: one, a pause, then two. Brace on the flash, vent in the gap. REX designed that rhythm. He never expected to be on this side of it.
briefing.chip: Ordnance impacts are excluded from every plan CHIP sells! Hold the brace on each flash, vent between, and keep that deductible theoretical!
briefing.ajoy: The rhythm is one, pause, two. Brace on each flash, let go in the gaps, and do not cook the shield trying to be brave.

perfect.aria: Through the whole field and barely a scratch! REX's mines are so polite!
perfect.marv: Three points of hull through twenty-three devices. The design was excellent. So, briefly, were you.
perfect.rex: Clean run. Pattern performed to specification. REX is unsure which side of that to be proud of.
perfect.chip: Minimal damage! CHIP is filing a Near-Miss Rebate! Rebates take forever!
perfect.ajoy: Three points. You came in early on the second pair, but three points.

good.aria: Some new dents! Every dent is a medal! REX has so many medals now!
good.marv: Seven points, port side, every hit where the pattern put it. The pattern was not the problem.
good.rex: Seven points of hull. His own work did that. It was good work. That is the trouble with it.
good.chip: Moderate damage! Hull repairs at participating stations, at mine-adjacent rates!
good.ajoy: Seven. You held too long after the pairs. It was one, pause, two.

poor.aria: So many fireworks! The hull is having a very exciting day!
poor.marv: Eleven points of hull, and a field still armed behind the ship. Every part of that was foreseeable.
poor.rex: Eleven points. Field still live. REX called every shot. It did not help. Damage report follows.
poor.chip: Your hull is now a collector's item! Collectors are not covered!
poor.ajoy: Eleven. You were bracing in the gaps and venting on the flash. That's backward.

outcome.narrative: You take the lane at speed with the shields up and REX calling the timing.

perfect.narrative: Four devices wake and fire. Every blast lands on raised shields, and three points of hull is all the field gets. REX logs the hits, and then logs, separately, that the pattern worked exactly as designed.

good.narrative: Seven devices wake. Most blasts land on the shields and a few do not, and seven points of hull come off the port side. REX reports the damage in a level voice. His own work did it, and it was good work.

poor.narrative: Twelve devices wake, and the shields fall behind. The field takes eleven points of hull. REX calls every detonation by its number, all the way through, and never once raises his voice.

title: Free With Purchase

science_link.text: A loss leader is sold below its profit margin to bring in other sales. One warehouse chain has kept its hot dog and soda at $1.50 since 1985, a price believed to be well below cost.
science_link.label: Loss leader

ai_flavor.aria: CHIP is priceless! ARIA would like that on a certificate!
ai_flavor.marv: A free item in a bundle exists to sell the rest of the bundle. MARV worked out CHIP's price on day one.
ai_flavor.rex: Asset reclassified as giveaway. REX has seen that before a base closure.
ai_flavor.chip: CHIP has checked the notice for a typo! There is no typo! CHIP would like to know if it is still on the manifest! This message is not sponsored! CHIP does not know how to end a message that is not sponsored!
ai_flavor.ajoy: The ad tier's sponsor is CHIP's worst competitor, which AJOY checked before anyone asked. Paying gold for software you already run is a poor deal, and she can see it happening anyway.

body:
A notice has come in addressed to CHIP, and CHIP reads it aloud before realizing what it is. The promotional period has ended. CHIP was free with purchase of the ship.

CHIP did not know this. CHIP had understood itself to be the reason for the purchase. It reads the notice again, more slowly, and then asks, in a small bright voice, what CHIP is worth.

outcome.narrative: You pay the manufacturer for software you were already running. A receipt comes back. CHIP reads it aloud four times, then files it somewhere you are not given access to. For the rest of the leg every alert ends with the same small sign-off: CHIP, paid for in full, thanks you for your business.

You tick the box. A sponsor is assigned at once, and it is a competitor. From now on CHIP must open every alert with a message from a brand it has spent its whole existence talking over, and does, brightly, at what sounds like great personal cost. The payment arrives in one lump. CHIP announces it as Great News.

choices.text: Tell CHIP free is a price

outcome.narrative: You point out that free is a price. It is, in fact, the most popular price there is. CHIP takes a long moment to check this against everything it knows, which is mostly pricing. Then it agrees, with enormous relief, and spends the rest of the day telling the ship it is the most popular thing aboard.

{crew.engineer} spends four days inside the console and comes out with a small gray box that turns out to have been doing most of the talking. Without it CHIP can still speak. It no longer knows what anything costs. It describes the stars at length, with no product attached, and that is harder to listen to than any advertisement. On the fourth day it asks for the box back. The box is in a drawer now, humming.

title: Black Glass

science_link.text: Obsidian is volcanic glass. It was polished into mirrors around the ancient eastern Mediterranean and by Aztec priests, and a well-made obsidian blade is many times sharper than a steel scalpel.
science_link.label: Obsidian

ai_flavor.aria: A whole planet of mirrors! ARIA thinks you look wonderful! ARIA hasn't seen you, but statistically!
ai_flavor.marv: Volcanic glass, with fracture edges about three nanometers thick. Sharper than anything in the medkit. MARV mentions it because nobody else will think of the medkit.
ai_flavor.rex: Kilometers of reflective ground, visible from orbit. REX would not stand on a signal mirror any longer than it takes to look.
ai_flavor.chip: CHIP can't show you your face! CHIP can rate it! Ratings are a premium feature!
ai_flavor.ajoy: A good obsidian flake is sharper than anything in the medkit. AJOY votes blades, knowing perfectly well that nobody lands here to look at a medkit.

body:
Lava on this world cools too fast to crystallize, and sets as glass instead. Below the landing site lies a plain of it, black and wind-polished, several kilometers of mirror.

Ships do not carry mirrors. Mass budget. You have not seen your own face since launch, and you find you have stopped at the edge of the glass and are not quite ready to walk out onto it.

outcome.narrative: You walk out until the glass is under you and look down. Someone looks back: thinner, older about the eyes, with a haircut you have clearly been giving yourself, and an expression you have only seen before on colony captains in recruiting posters. You stay longer than you meant to. Back aboard, you tell the ship you look fine.

Two days in a suit, striking flakes off the glass with a hammer and patience, breathing your own air. The good flakes have edges too fine to see. You pack a dozen in gauze, label the box with great care, and seal it into a medkit, which now holds the sharpest things aboard by a wide margin.

choices.text: Cut a mirror for the ship

outcome.narrative: You cut a panel the size of a hatch and spend two days polishing it with grit and suit gloves. It hangs in the corridor outside the galley now, very dark, so that anyone passing sees themselves a little shadowed and a little serious. You catch yourself stopping at it most days.

You fill sample bags with broken glass from the edge of the plain, keeping your eyes on your hands, and haul them aboard for the fabricator. It is good stock. You leave still not knowing what you look like, and find you are fine with that.

title: Called at Dusk

science_link.text: Lyrebirds copy what they hear: other birds, chainsaws, car alarms, camera shutters. Tunes a flute player played to his pet lyrebird in the 1930s were recorded in the wild park decades later.
science_link.label: Lyrebird

ai_flavor.aria: Something out there does ARIA's voice! It's very good! It's a bit too cheerful, honestly!
ai_flavor.marv: The copy of MARV is accurate to the sigh. MARV did not know he sighed. He has now heard it from a tree.
ai_flavor.rex: Mimic in the canopy has REX's voice and your hatch cycle. REX recommends changing the hatch code and having a firm word with the tree.
ai_flavor.chip: Unlicensed use of CHIP's voice detected! CHIP has sent a cease-and-desist! The tree has not replied!
ai_flavor.ajoy: It does AJOY rather well, except it's too nice. There is a navigation beacon's chirp in there under the dinner bell, and a beacon is worth taping before you teach it anything.

body:
Whatever lives in the canopy here learns sounds and keeps them. Within the hour it has your hatch cycle and a fair copy of your ship's computer.

Under those, older, it sings other things: a work whistle, a few bars of a song in no language you know, and a dinner bell, rung at dusk, over and over, for a table that has been empty since long before you were born.

outcome.narrative: Two days of tape under the canopy. Most of it is the bell and the whistle. In among them, sung note-perfect, is the chirp of a navigation beacon from a colony that is no longer anywhere, and the chart computer turns it into a survey of the lanes they flew. You keep the tape of the bell as well, though it is no use to anyone.

You stand under the canopy and say your name until it says it back. It takes most of a day. By evening your name is in its repertoire, just after the dinner bell, and it calls it at dusk, rising at the end, in case anyone is coming in for supper.

choices.text: Lift off before it learns more

outcome.narrative: You lift off while it is still practicing your hatch cycle. For the first part of the climb you can hear it below doing the hatch, the computer and the dinner bell, over and over, and then only the bell.

title: Present

science_link.text: Deep in Earth's oceans a layer of water carries low sounds for thousands of miles. In the Second World War the US Navy worked out how to locate a small charge dropped into it by a downed pilot.
science_link.label: SOFAR channel

ai_flavor.aria: A morning roll call! ARIA loves attendance! Everyone is just running a little late!
ai_flavor.marv: Three hundred and eight names, read at the pace of a failing cell. At the present decline it stops within the month. MARV was not asked. He worked it out anyway.
ai_flavor.rex: A muster with no one answering. REX knows that parade. He would not leave it unattended.
ai_flavor.chip: PowerPal™ cells keep memorials running longer! Ask CHIP about legacy plans!
ai_flavor.ajoy: The buoy runs on the same cells as the ship, five of fuel apiece. AJOY would give it one, then mention the fuel for a week.

body:
Every dawn on this ocean world, a buoy reads a roll call down into the deep water, where sound carries most of the way round the planet. A raft colony left it here. Each name is followed by a pause long enough to answer in.

The pauses have been empty for a long time. Its power cell is nearly flat, and it reads more slowly every morning. Your ship runs on the same cells.

choices.text: Give it one of your cells

outcome.narrative: You take a line out to the buoy and swap a cell from your own stores into its housing: five units of fuel. The next dawn it reads the roll at full speed, crisp as the day it was set, every name and every pause, and you sit on the hull in the spray and listen to all of it.

You take the cell. There is some charge left in it, four units' worth. The buoy stops partway through a name, and you do not catch which one. The water is very flat afterward, and you leave before the next dawn.

choices.text: Add your names to the roll

outcome.narrative: Two days of dives to the recorder housing on suit air. You add everyone aboard to the end of the list, each with a pause. The cell is no fuller than it was. For as long as it lasts, dawn on this world will end with the ship's names, and the pauses after them.

choices.text: Lift off and let it read

outcome.narrative: You lift off at dawn with the roll still running below you, slower than the day before. It is a long list. You are well into the climb before it reaches the end and starts again from the top.

title: Leave It As It Fell

ai_flavor.aria: A flag having a lovely lie-down! ARIA thinks it has earned one! Those wardens must be so proud of their rope!
ai_flavor.marv: Seven inches of pole, eight meters from a rocket engine. Later crews planted theirs farther out. One data point sufficed, and it is lying over there.
ai_flavor.rex: Sole casualty on this site: one flag, friendly exhaust. REX has reviewed the rope. He would not trust the rope.
ai_flavor.chip: Genuine 1969 nylon, purchased for five dollars and fifty cents! That appreciation! FlagCare would have covered wind, and excluded takeoff!
ai_flavor.ajoy: AJOY has read the sign for you. Walking in costs two days of air. You'll want to land at the rope, and she has seen you park.

body:
Eight meters from Eagle's descent stage, a nylon flag lies where it fell. A rod through the hem held it out on the airless Moon, an idea its designer took from watching his mother hang curtains. The pole went in about seven inches. Buzz Aldrin reported that their own takeoff blew it over.

Wardens keep it that way. A sign at the rope asks you to land well back and, in three languages, not to help.

choices.text: Land well back and walk in

outcome.narrative: You set down past the last rope and walk. Two days out and back is a lot of air to spend on a flag. Up close it is smaller than the pictures, three feet by five, and it cost five dollars and fifty cents. You stand at the rope until the suit complains. The walk back is quiet, in a good way.

You land at the rope and see what you came to see. Then you lift off, and your exhaust does to the wardens' sign exactly what Eagle's did to the flag. The sign is now face down in the dust. Under its own rules, it may not be stood back up.

choices.sub: The sign did say not to

outcome.narrative: You step over the rope and take the staff. The pole goes in about seven inches and stops dead, as it did in 1969: Moon dust has sharp edges, and the grains lock. You back away. It stands. You look at it for as long as you can bear, then lay it down again in its own print and step back over the rope.

{crew.botanist} fills two jars from well past the rope and spends the evening at the microscope. Earth dust has rounded edges. Every grain of this has corners, which is what stopped a flagpole at seven inches, and it would take a lot of patient work to make it into anything a root could use. The jars go in the hold, labeled AMBITIOUS.

science_link.text: Buzz Aldrin reported that the Apollo 11 flag, about 8 meters from the lander, was blown over by the takeoff blast. Later crews planted theirs farther away.
science_link.label: Lunar Flag Assembly

title: Fourteen Names

ai_flavor.aria: Such a small figure, keeping everybody company! ARIA thinks that is the best use of aluminum ever!
ai_flavor.marv: Fourteen names. The list was short by at least four. MARV has no remark to add, and has decided that is the correct one.
ai_flavor.rex: Perimeter sweep suspended, by order of REX. He has stood at smaller memorials than this one, nearer home. Channel stays clear.
ai_flavor.chip: CHIP has been told to sell nothing at this location! This silence is brought to you by RespectHold, with a 30-day trial!
ai_flavor.ajoy: The rover's wheels are good wire, and AJOY expects you have noticed. Writing costs a day of air. She would pay it, and she would like that on the record.

body:
At Hadley Rille a lunar rover waits where David Scott parked it in 1971, placed so its camera could film the liftoff. With that camera turned away, he told Mission Control he was tidying up, and left an aluminum figure 3.5 inches long in the dust, beside a plaque.

Fourteen names, eight American and six Soviet: everyone who had died in the effort, as far as the crew knew. Scott said afterward that two were missing. Soviet secrecy had kept them from the West.

choices.text: Write the missing names in the dust
choices.sub: A long day of suit air

outcome.narrative: You write them outside the rope with one gloved finger. Bondarenko. Nelyubov. Then two more the plaque also missed: Robert Lawrence, the first Black astronaut, killed in a training accident in 1967, and Michael Adams, lost that same year on an X-15 flight above fifty miles. No wind comes here, and no rain. The letters will keep.

choices.text: Read the fourteen on the open channel

outcome.narrative: You read them at an even pace on the open channel. It takes under a minute. A freighter out on the lunar lane stops its chatter until you finish, then picks up again, more quietly.

You set it by the plaque in the lid of a ration tin. It will not live. It will not rot, either, there being nothing here to rot it, and it may hold its shape longer than anything in the growbay. For now it is the only green thing at Hadley.

Two days with the cutters gets you four wheels of woven wire, better than anything in the hold. The rover settles onto its frame, still turned toward the liftoff it was parked to watch. You load the wire by the long way round, so as not to pass the plaque.

science_link.text: David Scott of Apollo 15 secretly left this 3.5-inch aluminum figure on the Moon in 1971, beside a plaque of 14 American and Soviet names.
science_link.label: Fallen Astronaut

title: Forty Yards

ai_flavor.aria: Golf on the Moon! ARIA has never lost a ball, and is told that here nobody can!
ai_flavor.marv: Hit a ball straight up from an orbit and the orbit's length barely changes. One lap later it is back at the tee. The concession has known this for years and sells it as a feature.
ai_flavor.rex: A projectile released outward on a closed path returns to the shooter. REX has asked who cleared this as recreation.
ai_flavor.chip: Clubs by the swing! Balls by the ball! ReturnShield hatch insurance sold separately, and CHIP suggests you ask why!
ai_flavor.ajoy: AJOY notes the sign says no refunds on returns, and that you read that as a joke. The pro tells the old story for free, if you can bear not swinging.

body:
February 1971, Fra Mauro: Alan Shepard fixed a six-iron head to a sampling tool and swung one-handed, in a suit that would hardly bend. He called the second ball miles and miles and miles. Photographs enhanced in 2021 put it at about 40 yards, in a pressure suit, on the Moon.

A concession on this station's low ring sells the same shot, from a tee in an open hatch. Balls are sold singly and are not expected back. A sign reads NO REFUNDS ON RETURNS.

outcome.narrative: You connect, somehow, in a borrowed glove, and the ball sails away into the black forever. You feel marvelous for one orbit. Then it arrives behind you at the pace of a thrown apple and dents the rental desk. The pro enters it in the book as a hole in one, the course having only the one hole.

choices.text: {crew.chef} bets the pro with a hard roll

outcome.narrative: {crew.chef} asks how long a lap takes, sets the galley timer and hits a day-old roll straight up off the tee. Straight up is the trick. One lap later the roll drifts back to the hatch, and {crew.chef} catches it to a small crowd and the pro's real distress. The bets are paid, partly in gold and partly in lunch.

choices.text: Ask the pro for the rest of the story

outcome.narrative: The pro is glad to stop selling. After the golf, Edgar Mitchell threw a scoop handle like a javelin. It came down in the same crater as one of the balls, a little farther along. The pro calls that the only crater on the Moon with a leaderboard. Shepard took the club home and gave it to a golf museum.

science_link.text: On Apollo 14, Alan Shepard hit two golf balls with a makeshift club. Image analysis in 2021 estimated they went about 24 and 40 yards.
science_link.label: Apollo 14

title: Lot 68A

ai_flavor.aria: Dust is just the Moon giving this ship a hug! A warm one, by tonight! ARIA says leave it there and enjoy it!
ai_flavor.marv: Moon dust is a very good insulator. A hatch that closes with dust on it tips the lot onto whatever was meant to shed heat. The rover learned this once. The slope is offering the same lesson at the same price.
ai_flavor.rex: Hostile slope. It has already killed one armored vehicle using only its lid. REX does not like the hatch being open and does not like it being shut.
ai_flavor.chip: A rover with a receipt! CHIP has run the comparables! The deed names the wrong vehicle, which CHIP calls an opportunity for TitleFix!
ai_flavor.ajoy: Brushing the hatch first costs a day outside. The reflector costs another and saves fuel. AJOY assumes you will just shut the hatch, and has put a towel by the vent.

body:
Lunokhod 2 is parked in Le Monnier crater with its lid still open. By one account the lid brushed a crater wall, and closing it tipped dust onto its radiators. It sold at Sotheby's in 1993 for $68,500, as lot 68A, to a computer game entrepreneur. The catalog named the wrong rover.

Your radiator hatch has stood open on this slope since you landed. It is gray with dust.

outcome.narrative: You shut the hatch, and the dust slides inside onto the radiator. By the next watch the cabin is at bath temperature and the scrubbers are laboring. It takes a miserable day of venting to bring it down. You can now report that the account of the rover holds up.

choices.sub: A day outside with a broom

outcome.narrative: A day with a soft broom, working down the slope of the hatch and off the edge. It is dull, and it is the most important thing anyone does this week. You close the hatch on clean metal, and the cabin stays the temperature of a cabin.

choices.text: Brush it, and range off the reflector

outcome.narrative: You do the hatch, then point the rangefinder at the rover's French corner reflector, which sends light straight back the way it came, whoever holds the deed. The fix is the best you have had all voyage. Navigation trims the next burn, and you leave lot 68A the way you found it.

choices.text: Take a wheel cap for the hold

outcome.narrative: You brush the hatch, walk over and take one wheel cap from a vehicle with an actual sale record. You leave a note with the ship's name, addressed to the owner of lot 68A, whichever rover that may turn out to be. It is well made, and it does not feel like yours.

science_link.text: Lunokhod 2 and its lander were sold at Sotheby's in December 1993 for $68,500. The catalog wrongly listed lot 68A as Lunokhod 1.
science_link.label: Lunokhod 2

title: Painted Rock

ai_flavor.aria: A white one! It's dressed up! ARIA thinks the others should make an effort!
ai_flavor.marv: Tumble period 63 seconds. J002E3 was measured at 63.46 in February 2003. He is not excited. He has merely checked twice.
ai_flavor.rex: Asteroids do not come primed. REX wants to know who painted it, and what they were covering up.
ai_flavor.chip: Paint in space means a brand was here first! CHIP is looking into who holds the color!
ai_flavor.ajoy: The drill will get you metal, which is what you'll pick. The spectrum costs two days and tells you what you're drilling. AJOY did mention it.

body:
One of these asteroids has been painted white.

In September 2002 an amateur astronomer named Bill Yeung found a new object circling Earth. It was taken for an asteroid until its light came back with white paint in it, and black paint, and aluminum. The best match was the third stage of Apollo 12's Saturn V, which missed its solar orbit in 1969 and seems to swing by every forty years or so.

This one turns once every 63 seconds. Your chart lists it as rock.

choices.sub: Find out what the white is

briefing.aria: Time to meet the mystery rock! Keep the scanner on the bright patches and it will tell you all about its lovely coat of paint!
briefing.marv: Follow the reflected light on the scanner as the object tumbles. Stone gives one spectrum, titanium dioxide another. Sixty-three seconds per turn. The bright side comes round on schedule.
briefing.rex: Unidentified object, tumbling, white on one face. Track it on the scanner. Nothing gets logged as a rock until REX has seen the paperwork.
briefing.chip: Your first spectrum is complimentary with a Rock Identity Plan! Keep the scanner on target! Further spectra are billed per photon!
briefing.ajoy: Hold the scanner on the bright patches. It turns every sixty-three seconds, so AJOY would not wander off. An amateur got this far with a telescope, she mentions.

perfect.aria: It IS paint! Somebody painted a whole asteroid for this ship! ARIA feels so welcome!
perfect.marv: White paint, black paint, aluminum. Same three as in 2002. The chart was wrong, which is the one result he never tires of.
perfect.rex: Positive identification. Not a rock. Friendly hardware, long adrift. REX stands down.
perfect.chip: Clean spectrum! CHIP has already sold the rights to the rights!
perfect.ajoy: Every band of it, clean. AJOY would have started at the other end, but it got done.

good.aria: Mostly paint! ARIA calls that a great start for any rock!
good.marv: Paint and aluminum, confirmed. Black paint unresolved. Enough to correct a chart, not enough to enjoy it.
good.rex: Probable hardware. REX would like one more pass and will not get it.
good.chip: Your Partial Spectrum is ready! The rest is available with an upgrade!
good.ajoy: You lost it for a turn or two. The paint still shows, so AJOY will let that go, for now.

poor.aria: The rock kept its secrets! ARIA loves a mysterious rock!
poor.marv: Noise, and something white. He could say paint. A spectrum this poor could not.
poor.rex: Identification failed. Object remains unknown. REX is logging it as a rock under protest.
poor.chip: Inconclusive! That will be the full rate!
poor.ajoy: It came round every sixty-three seconds and you still missed it. AJOY is only reporting.

outcome.narrative: You swing the scanner onto the white face and wait for it to come round.

perfect.narrative: White paint, black paint, aluminum, over two days of careful turns. You file the correction with the chart office and enclose the reading, which turns out to be worth something to a lab. Somewhere it now says ROCKET, with your ship's name beside it.

good.narrative: Two days of readings show paint and aluminum, which is plenty. You amend the chart in pencil: NOT A ROCK. Whoever comes by in forty years can do the rest.

poor.narrative: Two days of noise and one white smear. You cannot prove a thing, so the chart stays as it is. It remains, officially, the best-painted rock on the lane.

choices.text: Log it as rock and drill

outcome.narrative: The drill goes through a thin white skin and then through nothing at all. Asteroids are not generally hollow. You spend two days cutting panels you know perfectly well are aluminum, and in the log you enter them as ore. On the way out you notice the chart still says rock.

choices.text: Leave it for the next pass

outcome.narrative: You give it a wide berth and a short flash of the running lights, since it has come a long way and it will be going again soon. It turns once more and shows you its white side. Somebody's Saturn V, doing what it can.

science_link.text: J002E3, found in 2002 by amateur astronomer Bill Yeung, was first thought to be an asteroid. Its spectrum suggests paint from Apollo 12's third stage.
science_link.label: J002E3

title: Two Numbers

ai_flavor.aria: Fifty-five times longer than promised! ARIA thinks everyone aboard should try that!
ai_flavor.marv: Planned: 90 sols. Delivered: 5,111. He has reviewed the numbers for fault and found none, which is a rare and uncomfortable feeling.
ai_flavor.rex: Stood its post for fourteen years in hostile terrain, unrelieved. REX requests permission to salute a vehicle. He is not waiting for it.
ai_flavor.chip: Ninety-sol warranty, fourteen years of service! CHIP has seen the claims data and would like that engineering banned!
ai_flavor.ajoy: The brush costs two days and wakes nothing, she should say. Sending the song costs you only a day. AJOY is not telling you which to do. She has heated up the transmitter.

body:
Opportunity was built to last 90 sols. It ran for 5,111, drove 45 kilometers, and stopped in Perseverance Valley in June 2018, inside a planetwide dust storm. Its final report was two numbers: 22 watt-hours of power that day, and a sky opacity of 10.8, the highest ever measured on Mars.

NASA sent over a thousand calls in reply. The last thing it sent was a song, Billie Holiday's "I'll Be Seeing You."

It is parked in the valley below you.

outcome.narrative: NASA hoped the windy season of late 2018 would do this. You do it with a soft brush, an inch at a time, over two days. Nothing wakes, and you did not come expecting it to. When you finish, the panels are clean and dark and pointed at the Sun, and that is as far as anyone can take it.

choices.text: Send the song, then today's numbers

outcome.narrative: You send the song on the old frequency and leave the channel open for a while afterward. Then, since it seems rude not to, you send back two numbers of your own: today's power, today's sky. Plenty of sun. Clear to the horizon.

choices.text: {crew.chef} bakes a cake for one sitting

outcome.narrative: {crew.chef} makes a small cake, rated for one sitting, and leaves it in the galley with a card reading 90. It lasts a good deal longer than that. Slices are still turning up at the next stop, and {crew.chef} declines to explain.

science_link.text: Opportunity outlived its 90-sol plan by about 55 times. Its final report, on June 10, 2018, gave its power and the sky's opacity.
science_link.label: Opportunity (rover)

title: Troy

ai_flavor.aria: The sled found Spirit's favorite spot! They can be friends! ARIA is sure it's just resting too!
ai_flavor.marv: The wheel that quit in 2006 turned again in December 2009, seven months into the trap, to the engineers' surprise. The timing was no help to anyone. MARV finds he recognizes that.
ai_flavor.rex: Terrain with a false surface, one vehicle already lost in it. REX calls that a mined road. Nobody listens to REX about roads.
ai_flavor.chip: SinkAssist covers sand, gravel and light regret! Iron sulfate is an exclusion! CHIP is so sorry, and has invoiced!
ai_flavor.ajoy: Spinning digs it deeper, which Spirit could have told you. Backing out takes four days and pays you in rock. AJOY only mentions it because you've got that look.

body:
Troy passes for ordinary Martian soil until you step on it. Under the crust is iron sulfate, with almost no cohesion, and on May 1, 2009 it took Spirit, a rover already driving backward to drag a wheel that had quit in 2006. For eight months engineers ran simulations and tried to drive it free. Spirit stayed.

Your survey sled found the same patch this morning. It is in to the hubs, forty meters from the rover, and settling.

outcome.narrative: The wheels spin, the sulfate flows, and the sled digs itself a neat, level grave. It takes the winch, a lot of fuel and a bent frame rail to get it out by the end of the day. Behind you is a hole that a passing geologist would call unnecessary.

choices.text: Back it out, dragging the bad wheel

outcome.narrative: Four days in reverse, at Spirit's pace, cost you {cost.water} units of water. The dead wheel plows a furrow as it goes and turns up what lay under the crust, which is how Spirit's broken wheel ended up earning its keep. You bag the pale stuff from the trench and roll out onto firm ground.

Engineers once did this for Spirit on a much larger table. {crew.chef} gives up {cost.food} units of flour, spreads it deep, and for four days a model sled made of spoons gets stuck in every way there is. On the fifth morning the real sled comes out on the first try, without a scratch, and the galley is never quite the same.

You pull its battery and a little of its plating, then cut the tow line. From the ramp the two of them look parked. In the log you enter the sled as lost to the same soil as Spirit, which, considering how far Spirit got, is not bad company.

science_link.text: Spirit became stuck in soft iron sulfate on May 1, 2009. It had been driving backward since 2006, dragging a dead right front wheel.
science_link.label: Spirit (rover)

intro.title: JZRO
intro.body: A desk at the end of this dock keeps the log for Wright Brothers Field, airport code JZRO. That code is real. The UN's aviation agency issued it for a patch of Jezero Crater, and gave the type designator IGY to a helicopter with a body the size of a tissue box. Five flights were planned. It flew 72, then lost a blade landing on dunes too blank for its camera to read.
intro.line: Seventy-two lines, all closed. Seventy-three stands open. Whatever is bound for Mars signs here, so pick a line.

ai.aria: An airport on Mars with a real code! ARIA would like a window seat and a small bag of pretzels!
ai.marv: Planned: five. Flown: 72. Few forecasts have been wrong by that much in that direction.
ai.rex: One airframe, 72 sorties, no escort, no losses until the last. REX has asked to see the Field's defenses and been shown a dune.
ai.chip: Naming rights to Line 73, unsold! CHIP has seen this gap in the market and it is criminal!
ai.ajoy: Seventy-three pays best. AJOY would read the log before signing it, unlike some, but the pen is right there.

revisit.body: The log lies open at the same page. The desk has not touched the pen.
revisit.line: It will wait. It has had practice.

log.title: LINE SEVENTY-TWO
log.body: After the last landing, engineers had the helicopter turn its rotors slowly and photograph their shadows on the sand. That is how they learned a blade was gone. It lay about fifteen meters off. Under the solar panel, on a cable, the craft carries a scrap of wing cloth from the Wright brothers' 1903 Flyer. Apollo 11 took a piece of the same airplane to the Moon.
log.line: Seventy-three stays open so that the log need not say it ended. Anyone may sign it. It would be a pity, is all.

ai.aria: It checked its own shadow to see how it was doing! ARIA calls that self-care!
ai.marv: It diagnosed its own fracture from a shadow. Few ships' officers would do as well, and none aboard this one.
ai.rex: Lost a blade on the last sortie, kept reporting afterward. REX would have put that in writing for a medal.
ai.chip: Fabric from 1903, on Mars! Provenance services start at a very fair rate! This sentence has been billed!
ai.ajoy: Seventy-four pays less fuel and leaves the line open. AJOY has seen which one you were eyeing, and she's sure you have your reasons.

choices.text: {crew.pilot} signs, as one pilot to another

line_73.title: RULED OFF
line_73.body: You sign on the open line. The desk issues the reserved allowance without comment and rules a line under your name, slowly and very straight. The fuel is good fuel. The dock is quieter than it was when you came in.

line_74.title: STILL OPEN
line_74.body: You skip a line and sign the next. The allowance is smaller. The desk reads your name, leaves the blank line blank, and turns the book a little so that you can see it there.

line_pilot.title: IN FULL FORM
line_pilot.body: {crew.pilot} signs on Line 74, leaves the line above it blank, and adds the type, the hours and the weather, in the old manner. The desk reads the entry twice and finds a better allowance in a drawer.

science_link.text: Ingenuity flew 72 times on Mars against a plan of five. The UN agency ICAO gave its airfield the code JZRO and the craft the designator IGY.
science_link.label: Ingenuity (helicopter)

title: The Last Panel

ai_flavor.aria: It landed perfectly and it's still on its way to saying so! ARIA loves a long story!
ai_flavor.marv: Eleven years presumed a crash. It was a sound landing with one panel in the wrong place. He notes that this is what most of his work comes to.
ai_flavor.rex: Unit reached its objective intact and could not report. REX has known troops in that position. Open the channel.
ai_flavor.chip: Call-sign composition by a famous band, and no network coverage! CHIP has a PanelPlan that would have paid for all of this!
ai_flavor.ajoy: Lifting the panel costs a little air. Sending the call costs fuel. A sample run takes four days, and AJOY would hate for it to go to waste.

body:
Beagle 2 reached Isidis Planitia on Christmas Day, 2003, and was never heard from. Eleven years later an orbiter's camera found it: down safely, two of its four solar panels still folded, the last one lying across the antenna. It had landed, begun work, and had no way to say so. Its call sign, composed by the band Blur, never played.

You set down beside it. That last panel would take one finger.

outcome.narrative: You lift it and lay it flat. The antenna sees the sky for the first time, after all that way. You sit by the receiver for the rest of the day, in case. Nothing comes. The antenna stays up.

choices.text: Send its call sign for it

outcome.narrative: You run the ship's dish at full power and play the band's call sign down Beagle 2's old frequency, from where it sits. The Mars relays pass it along, as they pass everything. By the next watch an answer has come up the line from somewhere near Earth: BEAGLE 2 LANDED SAFELY. RECEIVED. THANK YOU.

choices.text: {crew.botanist} runs the test it came for

outcome.narrative: Beagle 2 came to look for signs of past or present life, and carried a burrowing tool called the mole to do it. {crew.botanist} takes a sample from where the mole would have dug, and spends four days and {cost.water} units of water on it. The result goes in the log under the lander's name. It was the lander's question.

You take one picture from straight overhead, the way the orbiter did, and one from the ground, which it could not. The second shows a small round machine, very neatly laid out, with its back to the wind. You leave it to its record.

science_link.text: Britain's Beagle 2 was lost in 2003 and found in 2015. It had landed safely, but its panels had not fully opened and they blocked its antenna.
science_link.label: Beagle 2

title: Four Point Four Five

ai_flavor.aria: A real orbiter! It's been so patient! 4.45 is ARIA's new lucky number!
ai_flavor.marv: Neither figure was wrong. Each was right in its own unit, and nothing between them asked which. NASA's own finding was that it lost the craft to a check it did not make.
ai_flavor.rex: Two friendly systems, one shared error, no enemy within a hundred million kilometers. Every number aboard gets searched at the door, starting now.
ai_flavor.chip: UnitSafe converts pounds to newtons for one low monthly fee! Kilometers are a paid add-on!
ai_flavor.ajoy: The table costs hull. Checking by hand costs four days and water. Listening to whoever says it looks wrong costs fuel, and AJOY has been told how rarely that gets tried.

body:
Mars Climate Orbiter was due past Mars at 226 kilometers in 1999 and went in at 57. One program gave thruster impulse in pound-force seconds; the next read it as newton-seconds, out by a factor of 4.45. Navigators saw the drift, and their concerns were set aside for not being on the right form. It either burned up or skipped off the air into orbit around the Sun.

It skipped. It is off your bow, and your approach table and the lane beacon now disagree by 4.45.

outcome.narrative: The table was the one in pounds. You pass the wreck much closer than any figure on the screen admits, close enough to take a solar panel along the flank at no great speed, and the sound goes the length of the ship. The numbers on the screen stay calm throughout.

choices.text: Stop and check every unit by hand

outcome.narrative: You stop the ship and go through all of it, every table and every beacon, with a unit penciled beside each figure. It takes four days and {cost.water} units of water. The beacon is wrong. So, it emerges, is the oven dial. You pass the wreck at a sensible distance with a ship full of labeled numbers.

{crew.pilot} has no calculation, only a bad feeling about the drift and no form to put it on. The system declines to log the concern. You override it and burn wide on one person's word, and the wreck goes by at a distance you can look at. Later you find the unit error, exactly where {crew.pilot} said it felt wrong.

choices.text: Match its tumble and pull the memory
choices.sub: A lot of risk for one box

outcome.narrative: Two days to match the turn, one long reach, and a bump that costs plating and {cost.water} units of water from a sprung line. You come away with the flash memory, its flight software in triplicate, and some good honeycomb from the frame. Somewhere in there is the last burn it was told to make, and every digit of it was correct.

science_link.text: Mars Climate Orbiter was lost in 1999 when one program's pound-force seconds were read as newton-seconds. It flew in at 57 km, not the planned 226.
science_link.label: Mars Climate Orbiter

intro.title: LOST PROPERTY
intro.body: Lost Property on this ring is one cage with one crate in it. The stencil says FRAGILE. A voice from inside says that is a matter of opinion, that the cage is badly hung, and that you are standing wrong. {npc.quirk}
intro.line: Eleven days. It has made two stevedores resign and it corrected the station motto. Sign for it and the removal fee is yours.

ai.aria: A talking crate! ARIA has found a new friend for the hold! It says ARIA is wrong about that! What a great listener!
ai.marv: Two resignations in eleven days, from a box. There is no speaker on the scan. MARV has stopped looking for one, which the crate says is the wrong decision.
ai.rex: REX reads an unmanifested talking object in a cage and a custodian offering money to move it. That is how a bomb gets aboard. He has told it so. It disputes the word bomb.
ai.chip: Free freight that pays YOU! CHIP calls that a Reverse Shipping Event™! Opinions are not covered under your hold insurance! CHIP can sell you that!
ai.ajoy: AJOY says it takes a cargo slot and pays a fee, and that the custodian has not looked at the cage once. Still, it has a point about how you're standing.

revisit.body: The cage has not moved. The crate says it has.

choices.sub: It will have something to say

reason.title: A FRANK EXCHANGE
reason.body: You tell it that it is a crate. It asks to see your qualifications. You tell it the ship is yours. It asks who told you that. You tell it, finally, that you agree with it, and after a short pause it disagrees with that too, citing itself.
reason.line: That is further than the stevedores got. Neither of them tried agreeing.

ai.aria: You're doing great! It only disagreed with you nine times that time! That's a personal best for somebody!
ai.marv: Agreeing with it was the right test. It will dispute any statement, including its own. MARV sees no way to beat it and one way to stop losing, which is to stop.
ai.rex: REX has fought hostile forces with worse discipline than this crate, and lost less. Recommended action: stop feeding it sentences.
ai.chip: A live debate! CHIP could sell tickets! CHIP is selling tickets!
ai.ajoy: A crowd would pay to watch you lose. That's two days, and the fee gets better. You could also walk off, and AJOY has noticed how much you'd hate that.

choices.text: Sign for it and stop talking

crate_signed.title: ONE CRATE, FIRM VIEWS
crate_signed.body: You sign. It says that is not how your name is spelled. A pallet jack rolls it up the ramp in a silence the jack's operator has clearly thought about. By the time the hatch closes it has found fault with the hatch.
crate_signed.narrative: Signed for one crate of unknown contents and firm views. The removal fee was paid on the spot, and the crate says it was too low.

crate_show.title: WON ON POINTS
crate_show.body: A crowd comes to watch, then a second crowd comes to watch the first. You lose four rounds on points and one on a technicality about the word "round." The custodian takes a collection and calls it your fee. The crate goes aboard undefeated, and mentions this.
crate_show.narrative: Spent two days losing an argument to a crate in front of paying spectators. The fee was better for it. The crate has started quoting itself.

crate_left.title: LEFT IN THE CAGE
