You sign. It asks for a rank and you give it. Every seal lets go at once, and the computer files the page and shuts off the lights while you are still in the compartment, having no further use for them. Two days by suit lamp brings out a fuel cell, plate and fittings.

Your name is on the page now.

cut.title: SEALS CUT
cut.body: Four days on suit air, one locker at a time. The computer reads out the replacement cost of each seal as you cut it and adds it to the {wreck.captain}'s account. You get most of what is there. The page stays on the console, unsigned, for the next ship.

struck_paper.title: IN PENCIL
struck_paper.body: The grower's daybook turns up under the chart table, left there after some argument. {crew.botanist} knows to look, growers having met computers. Four days of reading it into the record, in pencil order: what the computer said, and what it said later. The finding now reads: cause of loss undetermined. You know what it was. You leave the finding as it is. The seals open with a small, sour click, and you take what they held.

testimony.title: WITNESSES
testimony.body: You give it the number on the stern section's tag. A regulation tag is a filed document, and a filed document must be read in. GOOD WELDS. SORRY ABOUT THE WRENCH. YOU MADE IT THIS FAR. It reads them into the record, then the pizza order, under protest. Cause of loss is amended to: see attached. The seals let go, and two days later you have everything.

overwrite.title: AMENDED BY HAND
overwrite.body: You pull the panel and type one word over the finding. The computer vents the compartment, seals the hatch and reads you the penalties for falsifying a record, all four days it takes you to cut through to the lockers. Its docking clamp takes a strip off your hull on the way out. The page still says what you typed.

walked.title: LEFT ON THE CONSOLE
walked.body: You leave the page where it is. The hatches close behind you as you go, and you are in the airlock before you notice you have been walking quickly. You keep the ship alongside for two days, not boarding, not leaving. Then you go.

title: Fuel Felt

science_link.text: A real fungus lives on aviation fuel and water. Amorphotheca resinae is called the kerosene fungus, and it is a known contaminant of diesel.
science_link.label: Kerosene fungus

ai_flavor.aria: The ship has a pet! It's fuzzy and it loves the same food as the engines! ARIA calls that something in common!
ai_flavor.marv: Water has settled under the fuel and a fungus lives at the join, eating one and drinking the other. That is what the filter is coughing up. It is the only thing aboard with a clear plan, and MARV envies it.
ai_flavor.rex: Unidentified organism inside the fuel system, feeding on the fuel. REX considers the tank occupied territory and wants it retaken.
ai_flavor.chip: Fuel Felt™ is a known feature of the Standard Tank! Extended Filter Coverage is available! Coverage excludes fungi, felts and anything pleased with itself!
ai_flavor.ajoy: Flushing puts six units of fuel down the drain. The bigger tank or the condenser would have made this a quiet morning, and AJOY did bring those up. Please don't just keep flying on it, though you will want to.

body: Gray felt came up on the fuel filter this morning, damp, thick and faintly pleased with itself. A layer of water has settled at the bottom of the tank, and something has moved in where the water meets the fuel. It is eating the fuel. The engine has begun to cough on the hour, and the gauge and the dipstick have stopped agreeing.

outcome.narrative: The expanded tank has a cell nothing has ever needed. You pump across, let it stand overnight, and draw clean fuel off the top. Water and felt stay at the bottom and go out the drain together. You get back fuel you had already written off, and the cough stops.

choices.text: Run the fuel past the condenser

outcome.narrative: The condenser was built to pull water out of a gas and has no objection to fuel vapor. Two days later the tank is dry enough to starve the felt, and you have a drum of drinking water with a slight note of lamp oil. Filtered twice, you can hardly taste the note.

choices.sub: Lose what is at the bottom

outcome.narrative: Two days of draining, rinsing and swearing at a valve. A good deal of fuel leaves with the water, and the felt leaves with that. The tank is clean and there is less in it.

A new filter, then another by evening. The felt does not clear itself. It reaches the injectors, and the engine shakes the ship hard enough to start a seam before the stuff finally burns off. Nothing in the bilge is pleased with itself anymore.

title: You Have Been Selected

science_link.text: Spacecraft that sit too long facing the Sun overheat on one side. The fix is a slow roll along the long axis, called a barbecue roll, after a chicken on a rotisserie.
science_link.label: Spacecraft thermal control

ai_flavor.aria: Sunshine! In deep space! And someone picked this ship specially! ARIA has always wanted to be selected!
ai_flavor.marv: A twenty-meter orbital mirror once lit a spot five kilometers wide on Earth. This one is far larger and has a far smaller target. MARV gives the cargo bay until tomorrow.
ai_flavor.rex: A weapon with a billing department. It holds you in the beam, it names a price, it calls the price a service. REX has met this posture before. He wants it cracked.
ai_flavor.chip: Now that's marketing! No opt-in, no opt-out and a captive audience! CHIP would like to speak to this mirror's account manager, as a fan!
ai_flavor.ajoy: Fifteen gold for shade, or turn the ship like a chicken on a spit, which costs fuel and dignity. An insulated bay would have made this dull, as would a shield. AJOY only raises it because you were in the shop at the time.

body:
Daylight comes on in the middle of deep space, from one direction, at a price. A mirror the width of a small town has found the ship and is holding a patch of sun on it. Its beacon repeats: CONGRATULATIONS. YOU HAVE BEEN SELECTED FOR DAYLIGHT. SHADE IS 15 GOLD. NO CANCELLATIONS.

The port side is warm to the touch. The cargo bay is on the port side.

choices.text: Seal the cargo bay and sit tight

outcome.narrative: An insulated bay does not care where the heat comes from. You move the bunks and the rations in, pull the door to, and sit out the day at a pleasant temperature while the rest of the ship ticks and creaks. By morning the mirror has given up on you. Its bill is still running, and you cannot hear that in here either.

The emitter catches the patch of sun and throws it back the way it came. At that range a mirror is a very thin thing. A crack runs across the town-sized face, the beam goes out in pieces, and the beacon changes its message: YOUR ACCOUNT HAS BEEN CLOSED. You spend the day reeling in silvered film and frame.

choices.text: Roll the ship like a chicken

outcome.narrative: You put the ship into a slow roll along its long axis, so that no side has the sun for long. Two days of it, with everything loose making its way around the walls. Nothing burns or spoils, and at the end you feel basted. The mirror loses the angle and goes to bother someone else.
The patch of sun slides off the hull and away. A message follows: THANK YOU FOR CHOOSING SHADE. YOUR SHADE IS GUARANTEED FOR AS LONG AS YOU KEEP LEAVING. You keep leaving.

A day in the beam. Paint lifts along the port side, the growbay fans run flat out and lose, and {cost.food} units of rations turn in their wrappers. Then the mirror finds someone else to sell to, and the dark comes back at no charge.

title: Forty-Five Degrees

science_link.text: A beetle of southern Africa, where about 1.4 cm of rain falls in a year, drinks fog. It faces the breeze at 45 degrees and lets droplets gather on its bumpy wing cases until they roll down to its mouth.
science_link.label: Stenocara gracilipes

ai_flavor.aria: They're all saying hello to the wind! ARIA loves a team that shows up on time! Somebody here has a lovely padded post!
ai_flavor.marv: No rain on this world in the survey record. The beetles collect fog on their backs and drink it. It is the only sound engineering MARV has seen this voyage, and it was done by something with no budget.
ai_flavor.rex: Thousands of small units on every high ridge, all facing the same way, all holding a formation. REX has not ruled out that they are waiting for an order. The hut has been left unlocked, which he dislikes.
ai_flavor.chip: DewBack bottled fog is a concept with real legs! Six of them, per unit! CHIP is told the surveyor's notes may be proprietary, and would love to find out to whom!
ai_flavor.ajoy: Two days in the hut with the notebooks, or two days with tarps and a fuller tank. You'll say the water. AJOY would read the notebooks, since tarps only work on this ridge and a plan works anywhere, but it's your stale air.

body:
Along every ridge on this world stands a line of small dark beetles, faces to the wind, tilted at the same forty-five degrees. At dawn the fog comes in, and they drink it off their own backs.

A surveyor's hut sits on the third ridge. Outside it, in line with the beetles, someone has driven in a padded post at forty-five degrees. It is worn to a shine.

choices.text: Read the notebooks in the hut

outcome.narrative: Eleven notebooks, each more confident than the last. The surveyor copied the beetle's back onto a condensing plate, bumps and wax and all, and built it into a still that wrings drinking water out of plant scraps and mineral grit. The drawings are complete, and the fabricator can read them. The final entry says: It works. You can stop leaning now.

Two dawns of fog run down a waxed tarp and into the tanks, and the beetles shuffle along to make room. You leave the hut shut. There is a great deal of water, and it tastes of canvas and nothing else.

choices.text: Stand the seedling trays on the ridge

outcome.narrative: {crew.botanist} carries trays up the ridge and sets them among the beetles at the proper angle, after some discussion with a protractor. Two dawns of clean fog do more for the growbay than a month of filtered tank water. The beetles do not comment.

You lean. The padding takes your weight, the wind takes the rest, and when the fog comes you are part of something with a very simple plan. A little water runs down your collar. You can see how a person might have stayed.

title: Penitents

science_link.text: Penitentes are blades of hardened snow, over 5 meters tall in the Andes, that point toward the sun. They are named for a crowd of kneeling people doing penance. Darwin had to squeeze through a field of them in 1835.
science_link.label: Penitente (snow formation)

ai_flavor.aria: They're all looking at this ship! ARIA has never had so many fans! Forty million, and so attentive!
ai_flavor.marv: Sublimation sharpens each blade toward its heat. For all of history that meant the sun. The hull is a smaller source, but a much closer one. MARV has the closing rate and it is not a number anyone wants at lunch.
ai_flavor.rex: Forty million hostiles in ranks, all facing this position, closing without a sound. REX has waited his whole career for an enemy this disciplined. He would like to leave.
ai_flavor.chip: Forty million impressions and every one of them engaged! Ice can't be monetized yet! FrostReach is in beta! Please remain warm for the survey!
ai_flavor.ajoy: Stop being warm and they stop leaning, at four cold days. Or lift through the rows and pay in hull. AJOY would move the sun, if there were a botanist aboard with a spare lamp, but you've never liked that kind of idea.

body:
Forty million blades of ice stand on this plain, each taller than the ship, all kneeling toward the sun. You set down in a gap between two rows three hours ago.

The landing was warm and the hull still is. The rows nearest the ship have stopped pointing at the sun and started pointing at you. Measured against the landing strut, the closest blade is a hand nearer than it was at lunch.

outcome.narrative: Four days with every heater off. You sleep in a suit, the pipes freeze and split for {cost.water} units of water, and frost climbs the inside of the hull. On the third day the nearest blades lose interest and turn, a little at a time, back to the sun. You lift on the fourth with no feeling in your fingers.

briefing.aria: Hold on tight! It's like a big frozen high-five from forty million friends! ARIA believes in the paint!
briefing.marv: Lift now and the rows on the way up hit the hull one after another. Hold the brace through each strike and vent between them, or the brace fries. Five units of fuel either way. The hull depends on you, which MARV regrets.
briefing.rex: Hostile ranks overhead, close quarters, no way round. Hold the brace through each strike. Vent between. Do not cook it. REX will count them as they break.
briefing.chip: Every blade you block is a claim you never have to file! Hold that brace! Ice damage is an Act of Congregation, and not covered!
briefing.ajoy: Hold through the strikes, let go between them, and don't fry the brace. AJOY did say you could have waited four days. That was the other option. This one is loud.

perfect.aria: Through the roof! Only a little paint, and such a lot of applause!
perfect.marv: Every strike caught but two. Three points of hull. The rest of the plain did not notice, which is its best quality.
perfect.rex: Clean extraction. Light hull damage. Enemy ranks broken along one lane. He'll take it.
perfect.chip: Flawless exit! Paint touch-ups are not covered, as is tradition!
perfect.ajoy: That held. You could have done it with less shouting, but it held.

good.aria: You're out! The ship has some new ventilation features! Lovely and fresh!
good.marv: Eight points of hull, along the port side, in a line. The blades were not aiming. That is somehow worse.
good.rex: Out, with damage. Port side took the worst of it. Acceptable for an assault uphill.
good.chip: You're clear! Your hull is now a limited edition! Limited to the parts that are left!
good.ajoy: Not bad. Most of those were the ones you were told about.

poor.aria: You made such an impression on them! And they made a few on the ship! Everyone's connected now!
poor.marv: Thirteen points of hull. The brace fried at the worst moment available, and MARV has checked: there was no better one.
poor.rex: Heavy damage. Brace lost. This ship was rammed by scenery. That goes nowhere near the record.
poor.chip: Hull Replacement is on sale at participating stations! CHIP would not wait!
poor.ajoy: Well, you're off the ground. That was the main thing, and AJOY will leave it there, for now.

outcome.narrative: You open the throttle and go up through the rows. Eight points of hull and five of fuel, and a long glittering lane behind you.

perfect.narrative: You take the ship up on a steady column of fire and the blades go off the hull like thrown cutlery, one at a time, each caught and shrugged away. Three points of hull and five of fuel. Below you, a long bright lane is already refreezing.

good.narrative: Most of the rows give way. One line of them rakes the port side from the strut to the shoulder on the way up. Eight points of hull and five of fuel, and a scar that points, very slightly, at the sun.

poor.narrative: The brace fries in the second row, and after that the ship is simply being hit by a church. Thirteen points of hull and five of fuel, and you come out of the top with ice in places that were previously sealed. Nobody aboard feels forgiven.

choices.text: Walk a lamp out across the plain

outcome.narrative: {crew.botanist} takes the spare growbay lamps and a battery two hundred meters east, and switches them on. For a day nothing happens. Then forty million blades begin, in no hurry, to turn. You lift unobserved on the second day with the growbay short of light. Behind you a very small sun is burning on the plain, at the center of everything.

title: Collision Watch

science_link.text: Asteroids in the main belt are on average about 965,600 km apart. The belt is so thinly spread that uncrewed spacecraft have crossed it without incident.
science_link.label: Asteroid belt

ai_flavor.aria: Such a roomy asteroid field! ARIA thinks it's the safest place anyone has ever been frightened in!
ai_flavor.marv: MARV has the odds of hitting anything on this heading. They have a great many zeroes. He has read all of them out, to himself.
ai_flavor.rex: No contacts inside nine hundred thousand kilometers. That is exactly what a rock would want you to think. REX is keeping the klaxon armed.
ai_flavor.chip: Thank you for flying through a Premium Hazard Zone! Your hazard surcharge has been applied! CHIP regrets that actual hazards are not included!
ai_flavor.ajoy: The chart says densest part of the field. AJOY has looked out of the window. You can stand down and sleep, or spend two days and some fuel going to see the one rock, which you'll do, because you've come all this way.

body:
Collision watch is in its third day. The chart marks this as the densest part of the field, so everything loose is lashed down, the klaxon is armed, and the autopilot has been told to weave. It is weaving, with some style.

The nearest rock is nine hundred thousand kilometers away and leaving.

outcome.narrative: You unlash the mugs, disarm the klaxon and tell the autopilot to fly straight. It does so with a slight air of disappointment. You sleep ten hours through the densest part of the field, and nothing whatever happens.

{crew.pilot} takes the stick, kills the assists and flies the entire field by hand, rolling through a gap almost two million kilometers wide with the engines howling. It is a waste of fuel and the finest flying anyone aboard has ever seen, and there is no one to say otherwise.

choices.text: Go and visit the nearest rock

outcome.narrative: Two days and a real amount of fuel bring you alongside the only asteroid in the neighborhood. It is the size of a garage. You drill it anyway, and it takes the attention well. Its nearest neighbor sends no regards.

science_link.text: A poultice is a soft moist mass, often heated, held on with cloth. Poultices are used on horses to relieve inflammation, and may be used to draw pus out of an abscess.
science_link.label: Poultice

intro.title: HOUSE CALL
intro.body: Eleven kilometers of rock, warm along one side. The survey chart marks a cave. This cave has a lip, a dented service skiff moored to it, and a habit of closing twice a day. The call comes from somewhere behind the teeth. {npc.quirk}
intro.line: Good, a ship. Stay off the left side, that's the sore one. It has an abscess the size of your hold and I've been three weeks getting the poultice ready. I need someone to hold the jaw while it goes on.

revisit.body: The jaw creaks a little wider, then thinks better of it.
revisit.line: Still here. So is the patient.

ai.aria: A patient! ARIA adores a house call! And such a lovely warm side!
ai.marv: Eleven kilometers of rock with a pulse of about one beat an hour. MARV has checked it three times. The vet's estimate of the abscess is accurate, and so is the part about the mouth closing.
ai.rex: REX logged that opening as a mouth before anyone else did, and he wants it written down. Keep the engines warm and the ship pointed out through the teeth.
ai.chip: PetPlan for Minor Planets covers routine dental! Pre-existing jaws are excluded! CHIP has a form for the patient to sign, if it has a preferred surface!
ai.ajoy: Holding the jaw will cost hull. A cook would do the job without touching the ship, if there's one aboard. Or you can pay twenty gold and leave, and AJOY will say nothing about it, at length.

choices.text: Run a cable and hold the jaw
choices.sub: Two days, and it will pull

choices.text: Send {crew.chef} in to take over the pot
Ask what goes in a poultice

recipe.title: WHAT GOES IN
recipe.body: Soft things, the vet says, spread on cloth and held hot against the sore part until it gives up what it has been keeping. Bran, moss, boiled hide, the inside of anything that used to be alive. The vet's fabricator card scales it down to something you could put on a person. Along the lip, sloughed tissue lies in gray drifts, free to anyone with no sense of smell.
recipe.line: Same as any abscess. Bigger, and it can shut.

ai.aria: It's like a warm hug made of soup! ARIA would like one for every member of the crew!
ai.marv: As medicine it is four thousand years old and it works better than it deserves to. MARV has read the vet's card. The dosage for a person is correct. The dosage for this patient requires a crane.
ai.rex: The drifts are dead tissue, from a live hostile. REX will permit bagging it if nobody goes past the second row of teeth.
ai.chip: Artisanal Slough is a growing category! Bag it yourself and save! Odor is a feature of the premium tier!
ai.ajoy: Bagging the drifts is a day's unpleasantness for a load of biocomponent, and it gets you no card. The card is the thing you want. AJOY assumes you know that and are asking out of interest.

held.title: SAY AH
held.body: The cable takes the strain for two days, and when the jaw tries to shut, it takes a strip of plating off your bow as well. The vet goes in with a cloth the size of a mainsail. There is a long pause, then a smell, then a very deep sound you feel in the deck. Eleven kilometers of rock relaxes. The vet pays in kind: a fabricator card for the poultice, with a note on dosage for smaller patients.

cooked.title: NEEDS SALT
cooked.body: {crew.chef} tastes three weeks of the vet's poultice, says it needs salt, and takes over the pot. In goes the galley's whole seasoning shelf and {cost.food} units of food. It goes on hot at feeding time, when the jaw is down anyway. Eleven kilometers of rock sighs and goes quiet. The vet copies out the fabricator card with the corrections and asks whether {crew.chef} does weddings.

bought.title: CASH CLIENT
bought.body: The vet sends the fabricator card up on a line, with the air of someone moving a name to a different list. By the time you have pulled clear the jaw has shut on the job, and the call has gone quiet. You have a perfectly good recipe and a slight feeling of having left a farm by the back gate.

scrape.title: DRIFTS
scrape.body: Three sealed bags of gray slough go into the hold. The vet has no objection and charges nothing for it, which ought to have been a warning. The bags are sound. Everything you own smells of this rock until the next port.

title: Mr. Clock Is Flying With Us Today

ai_flavor.aria: A passenger! ARIA has never met anyone so punctual! He hasn't touched his dinner, so ARIA has upgraded him to a third seat!
ai_flavor.marv: MARV confirms the physics. A clock deeper in a gravity well runs slower, and the rider pays for the gap. He has worked out what this whole voyage has cost Mr. Clock. It is less than a blink. He finds that about right for the Company.
ai_flavor.rex: REX has been sharing a deck with a passenger who does not eat, does not sleep and ticks. He has asked twice for the seatbelt to be checked for wires. He suspects the second seat is for an accomplice.
ai_flavor.chip: CHIP admires any customer with two seats and no appetite! Mr. Clock is the Company's ideal traveler! Nanosecond Rewards™ are paid after a small seat-maintenance deduction!
ai_flavor.ajoy: AJOY has read the rider so nobody else has to. The pay goes up the closer you fly, and so does the hull bill. His meals are also being charged to the ship, in case a diplomat aboard would care to mention that.

body:
Mr. Clock has two seats, both paid for, and has not once complained about the food.

He is on the manifest as a Company research passenger: an atomic clock the size of a filing cabinet, belted in on the lower deck. His identical brother stayed in a basement at head office. A rider on his ticket has just come up. The heavier the neighborhood he is flown through, the further he falls behind his brother, and the Company pays the ship by the nanosecond.

This anomaly is a very heavy neighborhood.

choices.text: Skim the edge at the contract rate

outcome.narrative: Two days along the rim of the anomaly at a respectful distance. Mr. Clock falls a few nanoseconds behind his brother and gives no sign of minding. The Company remits by return signal, after deducting his meals.

You fly Mr. Clock down to where the frame begins to creak, hold him there for a day and bring him back up for another. It is the best two days of his career. Some of the plating did not enjoy them. The Company pays in full.

{crew.diplomat} points out that the Company bills his seats by the clock in the basement and pays his mileage by the clock in the seat, and that one of these is always in the Company's favor. Two days of correspondence follow. Head office concedes in a smaller font, and refunds the meals he never ate.

choices.sub: He has a schedule to keep

outcome.narrative: You steer around the anomaly and leave the contract unclaimed. By the next watch a blanket has appeared around Mr. Clock. The log does not say by whom.

science_link.text: In 1971 two scientists flew atomic clocks around the world on commercial airliners to test relativity, and the clocks came back disagreeing as predicted. The tickets included two seats on each flight for "Mr. Clock."
science_link.label: Hafele–Keating: Mr. Clock flies twice

title: Mid-Step

ai_flavor.aria: Tiny bears! In the water! ARIA has named the first four hundred! ARIA is running out of Stevens!
ai_flavor.marv: MARV has looked. They shut down, dried out and resumed without comment when wet. They have no idea how long it has been, and they have not asked. He would like to know how that is done.
ai_flavor.rex: REX reports several thousand boarders in the potable supply, eight legs each, ignoring all warnings. He has shouted at the tank. The occupants continued to advance.
ai_flavor.chip: Your water now includes Complimentary Bears! Extra protein at no charge! CHIP has just been told that is a charge! Bear removal is billed per bear!
ai_flavor.ajoy: AJOY says they are harmless and the water is drinkable, and she has already marked one clean glass for anyone squeamish. The filter clears them and tops up the tank. A jar would do more for spirits. She isn't naming any, so don't ask.

body:
Something in the water tank is walking.

Under the magnifier it is a fat little bear with eight legs, half a millimeter long, in no hurry. The condenser pulled dust out of this nebula, and the dust has turned out to be thousands of them, dried to husks. Water has reached them. Each has unfolded and carried on from exactly where it stopped, mid-step or mid-bite, with no sign of having noticed the gap.

The first one has arrived at the glass and is attempting to walk through it.

outcome.narrative: A jar goes on the galley shelf with a pinch of whatever grows in the sink drain. Under the magnifier they climb over one another with enormous seriousness. It proves impossible to stay angry while watching something that slow try that hard.

choices.text: Run the tank through the filters
choices.sub: Clean water, and more of it

outcome.narrative: You drain the tank through the fine filter and top it up from the condenser while you are in there. Two days later the water is clean and there is more of it. The bears are in the filter, dried back to husks, mid-step. They will not hold it against you, or against anything.

choices.text: {crew.xenobiologist} dries a batch and wakes it

outcome.narrative: {crew.xenobiologist} spends two days drying bears on a slide and waking them again, timing how long each takes to resume. None of them has lost its place. The sample flasks are worth keeping, and the notes run to a page headed WHERE WAS I.

science_link.text: Tardigrades can dry out into a 'tun' with no metabolic activity at all. In 2007, dried ones spent ten days in the vacuum of space on a satellite, and vacuum alone did them no significant harm.
science_link.label: Tardigrades: slow walkers

title: Locker Six

ai_flavor.aria: It's a time-release pantry! Future you is so generous! ARIA can't wait to meet future you! ARIA hears they have wonderful handwriting!
ai_flavor.marv: MARV has read the tags. Each item is signed out on a day that has not occurred, in ink that has not dried. He can say where this stock comes from, which is later. Who it is being taken from is a shorter question, and he expects the answer to come in person.
ai_flavor.rex: REX has secured aft stores against a hostile supplier who can forge the captain's signature. He has been told it is not a forgery. He has therefore added the captain to the list.
ai_flavor.chip: Buy Now, Pay Earlier! CHIP recognizes this locker as an unlicensed credit product! CHIP's cut is a percentage of tomorrow! Late fees apply retroactively!
ai_flavor.ajoy: AJOY says the supplies are real and the note means it. One item is a loan. All three is how you get a third note. She has moved the gaskets to the next locker along, since somebody had to think about the gaskets.

body:
Somebody has left a note on Locker Six, and the handwriting is yours.

IT RUNS BACKWARD. WHAT YOU TAKE OUT TODAY YOU PUT IN LATER. BE REASONABLE.

The anomaly has got into aft stores. Yesterday the locker held spare gaskets. Today it holds a water drum, a crate of rations and a fuel cell, each with an inventory tag dated on a day that has not happened yet, each signed out by you. You do not remember that. According to the note, you are not supposed to.

outcome.narrative: You sign the tag, which turns out to be already signed, in the same place, with the same slip of the pen. The drum goes into the main tank. A new line has appeared at the bottom of the note: THAT WAS YOUR ONE.

The cell slots in and the gauge comes up. Its charge history shows it has already been used, on this ship, for a burn you have not made. A new line has appeared at the bottom of the note: THAT ONE HURT.

You empty the locker and sign everything. By the next watch there is a third note, pressed so hard that the pen has gone through the paper: WE SAID REASONABLE. Scuffed footprints have appeared on the deck in front of the door, a long line of them, all your size, all facing in, as if someone had queued here. The stores are real. Sleeping near them is another matter.

{crew.xenobiologist} goes to put a numbered marble in the locker and finds it already there, with a chip from a drop that has not happened yet. Two days of careful notes later the door clicks, and the locker is full of gaskets again. There is one marble too many, and the number on it is higher than any you wrote.

You put eight nails through the door and go to bed feeling like a person with principles. By morning the nails are out and laid in a neat row on the deck. The note has been turned over. SUIT YOURSELF, it says, and the locker is full of gaskets.

title: Still Tuesday
alt_bodies:
Yesterday was Tuesday. So was the day before that, and you have begun to resent the cereal.

At the alarm the whole ship rewinds: the kettle goes cold, the dent you put in the bulkhead comes back out, the calendar returns to where it was. Only the pantry keeps count. Everything eaten on every Tuesday is still gone, and the shelves are starting to show it.

Today's breakfast is Tuesday's breakfast. You know this because yesterday's was, and the day before's.

The ship puts itself back at the alarm, down to the crumb on the table and the slow drip in the sink. The food does not come back with it. Shelves that were full on the first Tuesday are visibly thinner on this one, and the calendar declines to comment.

morning.title: TUESDAY
morning.body:
It is Tuesday. It was Tuesday yesterday as well.

Every morning the ship puts itself back: scratches heal, the kettle unboils, last night's log entry is gone. Then the alarm goes and it is the same breakfast. One thing aboard does not reset. What gets eaten stays eaten, and the pantry has been going down one Tuesday at a time.

ai.aria: It's Tuesday! ARIA's favorite! ARIA has said so every morning and meant it every time! This could be the best Tuesday yet!
ai.marv: MARV remembers every Tuesday. He did not ask to. The pantry falls a little with each one, and the calendar has stopped helping. He has kept a count, and the count is the only thing about this morning that has changed.
ai.rex: REX has cleared the galley every Tuesday so far and found the same toast in the same position. He considers the toast an extremely disciplined operative. The alarm is in custody.
ai.chip: CHIP's Tuesday Plan renews automatically! Cancellation requires written notice by Wednesday! CHIP looks forward to your Wednesday!
ai.ajoy: AJOY says food is the one thing not coming back, so perhaps stop eating it. She has left a note on the cereal. She left one yesterday too. The last page of the log is worth a look, not that anyone reads what she flags.

revisit.body: It is Tuesday. The page in the log has one more line on it, in your handwriting, and you do not remember writing it. Breakfast is as it was.

choices.text: Read the last page of the log
choices.sub: It is the only page left

choices.text: Spend a few hundred Tuesdays on the hull
choices.sub: No days lost, paid in food

page.title: THE LAST PAGE
page.body:
Everything resets but the last page of the log, which has been written on by hand, one Tuesday over another, in a hand that gets worse as it goes.

SMASHED THE ALARM. NOTHING. APOLOGIZED TO THE ALARM. NOTHING. BECAME A BETTER PERSON. NOTHING. BUILT A PIANO. LEARNED THE PIANO. NICE, BUT NOTHING. TUESDAYS GETTING SHORTER? IT COUNTS BREAKFASTS.

ai.aria: Your handwriting is so expressive! ARIA especially loves the crossing out! That's a lot of personal growth for one page!
ai.marv: MARV has compared the strokes. Every line is the captain's, and the shortening is real: this loop is running down, with about four days left in it. The last line is the only one that was never crossed out. He would believe it.
ai.rex: REX notes the page records an assault on the alarm, then an apology to it. He wants it understood that he does not apologize to hostile clocks. He has seen the piano and cannot account for it.
ai.chip: Handwritten logs are not covered by your Ship's Record warranty! CHIP can digitize that page! CHIP's offer resets every morning, so it's always the introductory rate!
ai.ajoy: AJOY points out the bottom line says it counts breakfasts, which she said an hour ago and also the Tuesday before that. Waiting works too, she supposes, if four more days of this sounds nice to anyone.

st_fast.title: WEDNESDAY
st_fast.body: You eat nothing. The plates stay clean, the kettle stays cold, and the whole of Tuesday passes hungry and cross. In the morning the alarm does not go off. The calendar says Wednesday, and the toast in the rack is the first new toast in weeks. You stand and look at it for longer than you would care to admit.

st_practice.title: A FEW HUNDRED TUESDAYS
st_practice.body: The reset takes back everything but what you know. So you learn the port seam, one square meter of it, over and over, until you can rebuild it blind in a single morning. Around the four hundredth Tuesday you skip breakfast to finish a weld, and the alarm stops. The seam stays done. The calendar has not moved at all. The pantry has, by {cost.food} units, one breakfast at a time.

st_omelette.title: THE OMELETTE
st_omelette.body: {crew.chef} has one pan, one tin of egg powder and all the Tuesdays anyone could want. {cost.food} units of food go into it, one failure a morning. Then comes the morning it finally comes out right, and {crew.chef} will not let anyone touch it. Breakfast goes uneaten. The alarm stays quiet. It is the finest thing ever made from powder, and everyone aboard has seen it.

st_wait.title: RUN DOWN
st_wait.body: You stop fighting it. Tuesday follows Tuesday, each a little shorter than the last, the final one barely long enough for toast. Then the calendar adds them all up with a small embarrassed click, and it is Saturday. The pantry is down {cost.food} units. You still know how every conversation at breakfast ends.

title: Long Odds

ai_flavor.aria: The air is all in one place! So tidy! ARIA has always said this ship just needed organizing! Also, ARIA has been dealt a perfect hand!
ai_flavor.marv: MARV confirms nothing here breaks a law. The second law only ever stated the odds, and locally the odds have stopped applying. He has worked out how unlikely this morning was. The number does not fit on the screen. The next rivet goes in under a minute.
ai_flavor.rex: REX reports that the ship's entire air supply has withdrawn to a defensible position. He approves of the tactic and not the timing. He wants to know who gave the order and what the rivets know.
ai_flavor.chip: CHIP has just won seven sweepstakes it never entered! LuckyBreak™ insurance covers neither kind of luck! CHIP has never been so fortunate or so worried!
ai_flavor.ajoy: AJOY has wedged a wet towel in the corner seam and saved you a spot. Reseating the rivets stops the leak. The burn gets out for a price, and waiting costs the most air. Also the coffee is boiling off your water, in case that seemed like a detail.

body:
All of the air has gone to stand in the aft corner of the hold.

Nothing pushed it. Every molecule aboard simply happened to set off the same way, which the ship computer says has always been allowed and has never once occurred. This morning's cards came out of the shuffle in suit order. A cold mug of coffee is boiling. Down the port side, every rivet has backed out one turn, by pure chance, and the first has just left.

You are in the corner with the air, breathing.

choices.text: Reseat the rivets as they go
choices.sub: Timed. Stay ahead of the odds

briefing.aria: The rivets are leaving one at a time! Let's catch them all! ARIA thinks they just want attention!
briefing.marv: Every rivet on the port side is backing out by chance. Each hole loses air that has only just agreed to leave the corner. The odds against the next one are enormous. It is coming anyway.
briefing.rex: Port side, multiple leaks, hostile rivets. Patch, then weld. They are moving as a unit and REX does not accept that as a coincidence.
briefing.chip: Rivet Retention is a subscription! Air loss is billed by the molecule, and they are all in one place, so it has never been easier to count!
briefing.ajoy: Patch, then weld, not the other way round. AJOY has laid the patches out along the port seam, in order, so there's no excuse. The clock is real.

perfect.aria: Every rivet home! ARIA knew they'd come back! And the cards are shuffling badly again! Hooray for bad cards!
perfect.marv: Every hole sealed before the air noticed. MARV has shuffled a deck to check. It came out in no order whatever. Normal service has resumed, which is the most he will say for it.
perfect.rex: All breaches sealed. Rivets are back under command. REX wants them watched.
perfect.chip: Flawless seal! Your rebate is in the mail, and the odds of the mail arriving have returned to normal!
perfect.ajoy: All sealed. The stern end would have been the place to start, AJOY thinks, but it held. The towel can come out of the corner.

good.aria: Most of the rivets came home! The others are on a journey of their own, and ARIA wishes them well!
good.marv: Most holes sealed. The air lost went out through the others by ordinary statistics, which is the route air is supposed to use.
good.rex: Leaks closed, losses taken. Several rivets escaped and are at large. REX expects them back with friends.
good.chip: A solid seal! Air loss billed at the standard rate! Rivets recovered by customers remain Company property!
good.ajoy: Two seams went late, and AJOY did point at them. The air is mostly back where it can be breathed.

poor.aria: The ship is so well ventilated now! Fresh space in every room! ARIA calls that open-plan living!
poor.marv: The rivets won. A great deal of very improbable air has left by the most probable route.
poor.rex: Port side lost the engagement. Air gone, plating loose. REX wants the surviving rivets questioned.
poor.chip: CHIP regrets that your Rivet Retention has lapsed! Reinstatement would have been very reasonable! Would have!
poor.ajoy: That was slow, and the air noticed. AJOY has marked the seam that will whistle from now on, so you can't say it wasn't mentioned.

outcome.narrative: You grab the patch kit and go down the port seam after the rivets.

perfect.narrative: You go down the port seam ahead of the rivets, patching each hole as it opens and welding behind you, and the last one goes home with a small, surprised click. Two points of air gone, two of hull. In the hold, the air comes out of its corner and spreads back through the ship as though nothing had been said.

good.narrative: You catch most of them. Two seams open before you can get there, and by the time they are closed the ship is five points of air and five of hull lighter. Somewhere aft, the cards have gone back to being shuffled badly.

poor.narrative: The rivets leave faster than anything has ever left anywhere. You seal what you can and the ship limps out of the patch with nine points gone from the air, nine from the hull, and a port seam that will whistle from here on.

outcome.narrative: You light the drive, and for the first time in the history of rocketry a measurable share of the exhaust happens to go forward. It is a long, undignified burn, mostly sideways, and the rivets keep leaving all the way. Then a shuffle comes out in no order at all, and the air wanders back out of its corner.

choices.text: {crew.engineer} tips the scrap down the ladder
choices.sub: Let the odds do the fit

outcome.narrative: Where anything may land any way, {crew.engineer} pours a bin of scrap down the ladder well. It lands as a working rivet gun. The second bin lands as nine hundred rivets, already seated. Two days and a good deal of air later the seam is better than new, and a third bin, tried out of greed, has landed as a violin. It is out of tune, which is a comfort.

choices.text: Stay in the corner until the odds even out

outcome.narrative: You stay with the air. Over four days the odds drift back toward the usual, and it wanders out one room at a time, thinner than it went in. The coffee takes {cost.water} units of water with it before it agrees to stop boiling. You come out of the corner with a crick in the neck and a deep distrust of cards.

science_link.text: The second law of thermodynamics turned out to be statistical. There is always some nonzero chance that entropy will fall on its own, and the fluctuation theorem gives that chance exactly. It shrinks exponentially as the system grows.
science_link.label: Fluctuation theorem: the second law's fine print

title: Collect Call

ai_flavor.aria: It's us! We've grown so much! ARIA would love to say hello to ARIA! She has so much to tell herself!
ai_flavor.marv: MARV has matched the hull, the voice and the fuel curve. That is this ship, on a day not yet reached, and no version of events says otherwise. He has also read the message from its MARV. It says the calculation is correct and to stop showing it to people.
ai_flavor.rex: REX has a firing solution on the ship's own future and has been asked to put it down. A vessel with our codes, our guns and our tactics is the worst thing he has ever had to look at. It has him targeted as well, for the same reasons.
ai_flavor.chip: CHIP must advise that this is a collect call! Charges are reversed to the caller, who is you! Your account is now in dispute with your account! CHIP wins either way!
ai_flavor.ajoy: AJOY says their tanks are dry and the request is real. Pumping costs water. An engineer could fix their condenser for hull and days. She has already cracked the pump valve. The other AJOY agrees with her, and that is the part she doesn't like.

body:
You have not sent a distress call, and this one is in your voice.

The ship comes out of the anomaly sideways with its port lights dead. Same hull, same stains, a good many more scars. Its log tag carries a date that has not happened. Its tanks read dry. The text comes up in your own phrasing:

YOU KNOW HOW MUCH. WHATEVER YOU DO NOW IS WHAT WAS DONE TO US. WE REMEMBER HOW THIS GOES. WE WOULD LIKE YOU TO FIND OUT FOR YOURSELF.

choices.text: Pay back what you took from Locker Six

outcome.narrative: The tag in Locker Six still has your signature on it, twice. You put {cost.water} units of water in the locker and shut the door. It is not what you took, and the tag has no column for that. Across the gap something clangs into the other ship's hold, exactly where it has been missing from. Their lights steady. The text comes up once more: THAT'S ALL IT EVER WAS. BE REASONABLE.

For two days the tanks go down on your side by {cost.water} units and up on theirs, and a familiar voice says thank you in the flat way you say it when you mean it. The lights steady. The ship turns back into the anomaly without saying where it is going. You do not ask, and you notice that it knew you wouldn't.

choices.text: {crew.engineer} goes across to fix their condenser

outcome.narrative: {crew.engineer} crosses with a toolbag and is met at the lock by {crew.engineer}. For four days they rebuild the condenser together and criticize each other's welds, and a strip of your plating goes across to finish the job. The condenser runs. Both of them have asked you to note in the log that the other one's work was poor.

You cut the channel and burn past, close enough to read the name on the hull. It is your name. The other ship does not chase you. Its last text arrives a minute after you stop listening, and it is the thing you always say when you have decided not to be angry. Its lights go out from the bow back, in the order you would have shut them down.

science_link.text: The Novikov self-consistency principle holds that if travel into the past is possible, any event that would change the past has a probability of exactly zero. Whatever happened is what happens.
science_link.label: Novikov self-consistency principle

title: Closing Ceremony

ai_flavor.aria: A banner! Chairs! They knew we were coming! ARIA has always wanted to be the last ones at a party! So much room to dance!
ai_flavor.marv: MARV confirms this is after the last star. The ship's own stores are the only useful energy left anywhere, and there is nothing to steer by. Given this long, chance will build any door. He has priced waiting for one. He would look instead.
ai_flavor.rex: REX has counted the chairs and found nobody in charge, which is how these things start. Every mind out here has asked to sit by the ship. He is not running a shelter. He wants the exit found and the perimeter held against the chairs.
ai_flavor.chip: CHIP regrets that this is the Last Available Venue! No refunds after the end of time! FinalHall™ charges per chair, and there will be more chairs!
ai_flavor.ajoy: AJOY says the scanner finds the exit fastest, the boiler brings one on for a price in water, and sitting here costs two weeks of air. She has told the nearest mind that seat is taken. It has gone out, so she supposes that settles it.

body:
THANK YOU FOR COMING, says the banner. It is made of nothing in particular and was assembled by chance, like the row of folding chairs beneath it.

Past the chairs there are no stars. The void has let you out after the last of them, into an even, lukewarm dark with nothing left to steer by. You are the warmest thing remaining. Minds keep forming near the hull, thanking you for the heat, remembering childhoods that never happened, and going out.

Given long enough, this dark produces anything. A fire exit, for instance.

briefing.aria: There's a fire exit in here somewhere! Let's find it before the party winds down! It's such a lovely party!
briefing.marv: Chance is assembling everything out there, one thing at a time. Find the pattern that is turning into a door, and go through it before it turns into something else.
briefing.rex: Sweep for the exit. Ignore the chairs. REX has been watching the chairs. Do not let them get behind the ship.
briefing.chip: One (1) exit included with your stay! Exits located after the end of time are billed at double! CHIP checked with Legal, and Legal has gone out!
briefing.ajoy: It's on the scanner, among a great many things that are not doors. AJOY has already marked the ones that are definitely a shoe. Look properly, and quickly.

perfect.aria: We found the door! We stayed right to the end and still got out early! Best party ever!
perfect.marv: A clean exit from the end of everything, and four seconds have passed. MARV can now report that the universe ends exactly as he said it would.
perfect.rex: Door taken. Chairs left holding the field. One chair came with the ship. REX has it under guard.
perfect.chip: Exit located! Your FinalHall™ deposit is forfeit, as agreed by you, in a future that is now over!
perfect.ajoy: The first door out. AJOY had it marked on the second sweep, but well done on the third. That chair is in the cargo clamp and she is not moving it.

good.aria: A door! A slightly wrong door! ARIA loves an entrance with character!
good.marv: That door was a poor copy of a door. Chance had only so long to work with, in the sense that it had forever and the ship did not.
good.rex: Exit forced under poor conditions. Hull took fire from a door frame. REX did not expect to say that.
good.chip: Exit located! Frame-scrape damage is part of the Standard Door Experience! Not covered!
good.ajoy: That door was a rough draft. There was a better one further along, which AJOY had marked. Still, stars.

poor.aria: We left so dramatically! That's how you know it was a good party!
poor.marv: The scanner found a dozen paintings of doors. The real one formed late and shut early. Fourteen of fuel, eighteen of hull. The universe ended as it lived.
poor.rex: Withdrew under door fire. Heavy losses. There will be an inquiry, REX will conduct it, and the chairs will answer.
poor.chip: Your exit was processed as an eviction! Eviction fees apply! They would have applied sooner, but there was no sooner!
poor.ajoy: Those were paintings. AJOY did mark them. The real door nearly took the ship in half, and she'd like that warning read next time.

outcome.narrative: You set the scanner to look for anything in the dark shaped like a way out.

perfect.narrative: You find it on the third sweep: a green sign forming out of nothing, over a door still making up its mind. You are through before it finishes. The ship comes out into ordinary stars about four seconds after it left, six points of fuel down, four of hull, with a folding chair caught in the cargo clamp. The chair is made of nothing on any chart.

good.narrative: The door you find is a poor copy, and it opens partly onto the wrong side of itself. You get through at a scrape. Ten points of fuel and ten of hull later the stars are back, and you have never been so pleased to see anything burn.

poor.narrative: The scanner finds a dozen doors, all painted on. The real one forms behind you, late, and starts to close while you are still going through it. Fourteen points of fuel, eighteen of hull, and the ship comes out with the distinct feeling of having been asked to leave.

choices.text: {crew.engineer} vents the boiler at the dark

outcome.narrative: Everything out here forms thickest near the warm hull, so {crew.engineer} gives the dark more to work with: {cost.water} units of hot water, vented in one long plume. Over four days it fills the local universe with the only weather it has had in a very long time, and a door condenses out of it, slightly damp. It is a tight fit, and the hull pays for it.

choices.text: {crew.diplomat} polls the minds for the way out

outcome.narrative: Each mind that forms has a complete and detailed memory of the way out, and every one is false. {crew.diplomat} cracks the vents to be heard, at some cost in air, and takes a poll. Four days and several thousand brief respondents later, the wrong answers turn out to be wrong in a consistent direction, and you fly the other way. The last respondent thanks you for the chat and asks how it went.

choices.text: Sit down and wait for a door

outcome.narrative: You sit down to wait. Outside, more years go by than there are numbers for. Aboard it is fourteen days of thin air and {cost.food} units of food, watching the dark try things: a spoon, a shoe, half a staircase. On the last day it produces a door, with a fire bucket beside it and a small printed apology.

science_link.text: A Boltzmann brain is a thought experiment: over a long enough time, random fluctuations could assemble any structure at all, including a lone mind complete with false memories. Physicists use it to test theories, mostly by trying to avoid it.
science_link.label: Boltzmann brain: a mind by accident

title: Not on the Schedule

ai_flavor.aria: Earth! From the OUTSIDE! It looks so healthy from here! ARIA is choosing to take that as a very good sign!
ai_flavor.marv: The burn window is ninety seconds wide. Earth will be up a good deal longer than that. One of the two is going to be missed, and MARV would rather it were the view, which he accepts is the unpopular answer.
ai_flavor.rex: Shuttle on the port side, clear approach, blinds down. Either its passengers have seen this before or they are hiding something. REX is keeping both files open.
ai_flavor.chip: Earthrise is a registered experience of LunarLoop Tours! Viewing from a non-tour vessel attracts a courtesy fee! CHIP has applied for a waiver, and the waiver has a fee!
ai_flavor.ajoy: Slipping the burn by one orbit costs about two of fuel. Spend it. Also, the hull camera is still set to gray, since nobody else was going to say so.

body:
Your flight plan for the swing round the Moon is a column of burns and coasts, timed to the second. It does not mention that Earth comes up over the Moon's edge halfway through. The crew of Apollo 8, the first people to see it happen, had the same trouble: one joked that the picture wasn't scheduled, and another called for color film.

A commuter shuttle flies this loop beside you twice a week. Its blinds are down.

From here, Earth looks fine.

outcome.narrative: You let the burn go by and take the next one, which costs two of fuel to set right, and spend the orbit at the forward window. Earth climbs over a gray edge, blue and white, with weather on it. Whoever is aboard finds where they were born, or near enough, and points.

Navigation has no use for color, so the hull camera has never needed it. By the time you find the setting, Earth is clear of the edge and climbing. You get it anyway, blue over gray, and print it for the galley wall, where it is the only thing in the galley that is not beige.
The burn goes in on the second and the ship comes round the Moon with two of fuel to spare. Earth rises behind you, on the side with no windows. The plan was right about everything it mentioned.

science_link.text: Apollo 8's crew were the first people to see Earth rise over the Moon, in 1968. The photograph was not on the schedule, and they scrambled for color film.
science_link.label: Earthrise

title: Spent Gunpowder

ai_flavor.aria: The Moon followed everyone home! ARIA thinks the whole ship smells like a celebration! Fireworks every day!
ai_flavor.marv: The scrubbers were rated on Earth dust, which is rounded off by wind and water. Moon dust is glass with its corners on. At this rate the filters will not last the leg, and MARV did not need long to see it.
ai_flavor.rex: Everything aboard smells of a firing range. REX has searched for the firing range three times. He will search again at the next watch.
ai_flavor.chip: DustOut™ Lunar Grade is the leading answer to Moon dust! It is not aboard! CHIP does have a magnet, and will rent it to you by the hour!
ai_flavor.ajoy: Much of that dust carries iron, so a magnet lifts a good part of it. It's slow. It is also the only option that doesn't end with the seals whistling.

body:
Yesterday's walk on the surface came back aboard in the seams. Moon dust is nothing like dust at home: each grain is a chip of glass, sharp, and it sticks to whatever it lands on. It is in the suits, the air filters and the bunks, and it smells and tastes of spent gunpowder.

On Apollo's sample bottles it wore through the seals and let the air in. Your seals are not as good as those were.

choices.text: Go over everything with a magnet

outcome.narrative: Much of the dust has flecks of iron in its glass, so for four days everything aboard gets a slow pass with a magnet from the parts bin: suits, filters, bunks, the galley table. It comes away gray and furred. By the end the ship smells only of itself, and the magnet is kept in a jar.

choices.sub: Quick, and the air goes too

outcome.narrative: Suits on, you open the cabin to vacuum and let the air carry the loose dust out with it, then bleed fresh air back in from the tanks. {cost.o2} points of oxygen leave in a gray plume. Whatever had already stuck to something stays stuck, but there is much less of it to breathe.

You leave it. Over the next leg the dust works into the door seals and the scrubbers, every meal crunches faintly, and the whole ship smells of a firing range. By the next stop two seals are scored through and whistling, and the scrubbers sound like gravel in a can.

science_link.text: Lunar dust is made of sharp, very sticky grains that smell and taste of spent gunpowder. It wore through the seals of the Apollo sample bottles.
science_link.label: Lunar regolith

title: Radio Shadow

ai_flavor.aria: A whole observatory just listening to the universe! ARIA will be SO quiet! ARIA is practicing now! This is ARIA practicing!
ai_flavor.marv: Switching everything off includes the scrubber fans, so it costs air. Going round costs fuel. Crossing loud costs nothing, except that this ship will be all the dish hears for two nights. MARV has rated that outcome. Poorly.
ai_flavor.rex: Two days in a shadow with no beacon and no channel, because a buoy asked nicely. REX has known ambushes to open with less. He will be awake for both days.
ai_flavor.chip: Silence is a premium product! Two days of it would retail at a figure CHIP is not allowed to broadcast in this zone! CHIP will announce the price on the far side!
ai_flavor.ajoy: The scrubbers hum, so silence costs a little air. Worth knowing what in the growbay is humming, too, before you decide what else to switch off.

body:
Behind the Moon is the quietest place a radio can go. The Moon stands between it and every transmitter on Earth, which is why someone has built a listening dish in a crater over there, and why a buoy at the edge of its shadow asks every passing ship, politely and on a loop, to switch everything off.

Crossing the shadow takes two days. Everything means the beacon, the open channel, the outward chatter of the ship's computer and anything else that hums.

choices.sub: Fans and all, for two days

outcome.narrative: For two days the ship is dark on every band, scrubber fans included, and the air goes stale enough to cost {cost.o2} points of oxygen. People talk in whispers, though nothing aboard could hear them shout. On the far side the buoy changes its loop to a thank-you and sends a picture: a patch of sky, very old and very faint, with no ship in it.

You burn round the rim of the shadow with every radio running. Four of fuel is what it costs to go the long way past a quiet place. The buoy thanks you for your consideration, on a loop, in the same voice it uses for everyone.

Two days, beacon on, channel open. On the far side the buoy has a new recording, made for you. It is the dish's last two nights, and it is entirely your ship: the beacon's ping, the cargo manifest, and the computer reading the terms of service to an empty channel. They thought you should have a copy.

{crew.botanist} traces the hum to the growbay: on the radio the lamp drivers are louder than the beacon. The bay goes dark for the two days of the crossing, and anything growing in it goes two days without light. The beacon stays on, the fans keep turning, and the dish gets two quiet nights anyway, and says so.

science_link.text: The Moon blocks radio from Earth, so its far side is thought to be a good place for radio telescopes, if the area around them is kept free of other transmitters.
science_link.label: Far side of the Moon

title: One in Ten Thousand

ai_flavor.aria: One in three hundred means two hundred and ninety-nine lovely chances! ARIA has counted them! ARIA has named several!
ai_flavor.marv: Twelve crossings at one in three hundred each comes to about one in twenty-five over the week. The corridor's own line is one in ten thousand. The commuters worked that out before anyone aboard, which MARV notes without pleasure.
ai_flavor.rex: Invisible enemy, fixed patrol route, no command structure, no surrender. REX has faced worse odds. He has not faced anything he could not see.
ai_flavor.chip: DebrisGuard covers impacts from cataloged objects only! Everything smaller is an Act of Physics! Premiums remain payable in full!
ai_flavor.ajoy: Tail-first puts the hits on the engines, which matter less than the window. The next lane already has every commuter in it, which is worth a thought before you join them.

body:
This near home, the debris office posts a forecast every morning, and this morning's names your ship. A cloud from an old breakup crosses your lane a dozen times over the next few days, and each crossing carries a one-in-three-hundred chance of a hit from something too small to see.

The corridor's rule is to move at one in ten thousand. All around you the commuter shuttles have already moved, at once, into the next lane, which was full.

outcome.narrative: You burn into the next lane with half the commuter traffic in the corridor, all of it dodging the same cloud, which means everyone is dodging everyone. It costs five of fuel. A fleck of somebody's paint, too small for any catalog, leaves a pit a millimeter wide in the forward window, at eye level, for the rest of the voyage.

The old shuttles flew tail-first through the worst of it, so that whatever hit them hit the parts they could spare. You turn the ship round and hold course with the engine bells to the cloud. Each crossing, something rings off the stern. Seven points of hull, most of it round the nozzles, and the engine burns two of fuel rougher than it should.

choices.text: Hold course and shelter in the hold

outcome.narrative: Each time the cloud comes round, everyone aboard suits up and waits in the hold with the hatch shut, because it is the safest room on the ship, which is not saying a great deal. Twice something gets through: once into the hull, once into a tank of suit air. Both times the hold was empty of anything that bleeds.

choices.text: Wait for the cloud to spread
choices.sub: A long week at the edge

outcome.narrative: You stop at the edge of the lane and let the cloud thin. Eight days on station cost {cost.water} units of water and {cost.food} of food. When the office finally lifts the warning, it posts the corridor's figure for the year alongside it, and the figure is a little higher than last year's.

{crew.pilot} loads every tracked piece in the cloud and flies each crossing by hand, slipping past them all with a little to spare. It is beautiful flying, and it does nothing about the pieces too small to track, which are most of them. Three of fuel, three of hull, and {crew.pilot} skips a meal over it.

science_link.text: The International Space Station dodges debris with more than a one-in-10,000 chance of hitting it. Three times, late warnings sent its crew to shelter in their Soyuz instead.
science_link.label: Space debris

title: Polls Have Closed

ai_flavor.aria: An ELECTION! ARIA loves democracy! ARIA has read both platforms and agrees with each of them completely!
ai_flavor.marv: Both messages use your name. Both were recorded four months ago for every ship on the Mars run. The candidates have spent the time since finding out how it went, which is more than anyone aboard can say.
ai_flavor.rex: Two factions, one water supply, a disputed count. REX would like to land after it is settled, by whatever means it gets settled.
ai_flavor.chip: Today's edition is available at Premium tier! The free tier is also news, in the sense that it used to be! CHIP recommends upgrading at once!
ai_flavor.ajoy: The paid edition carries the current approach chart, which the free one leaves out. That is not the same as saying it's worth the price. It is in there, though.

body:
News from the colony is free if you will wait for it. Radio would carry it in minutes, but the free tier goes out in bulk when bandwidth is cheap, and this morning's bundle is four months old.

It is an election. One candidate for the landing council promises every arriving ship a tank of water. The other promises to charge arriving ships for the water they drink. Both have sent long, sincere messages to you personally. The polls closed some time ago.

outcome.narrative: The paid edition arrives in minutes. The election is undecided. Ballots from ships in transit keep arriving, and each one reopens the count, and there is a third candidate now who wants to stop counting. Folded in the back is a corrected approach chart that saves you three of fuel.

choices.text: Donate to the water candidate: 5 gold

outcome.narrative: The donation reaches the campaign in minutes and four months after the vote. Whether or not the candidate won, they keep their word: a relay drone finds you before the day is out with a dented tank of water and a sticker reading A TANK FOR EVERY SHIP.

Voting takes most of an afternoon, because the ballot runs to eleven pages and has a section on irrigation. It reaches the colony in minutes. Under a rule still on the books, a ballot that arrives after the polls close is held over, and counted, in the next election.
You delete it. Overnight it is replaced by the next bundle, which is three months old and mostly about the first.

title: Please Hold for the Next Part

ai_flavor.aria: A conversation that lasts for DAYS! ARIA loves talking! ARIA has already drafted answers to the next three questions!
ai_flavor.marv: Nine minutes each way, so a single yes costs eighteen. The officer spoke for sixteen without a breath. MARV respects anyone who has given up expecting to be interrupted.
ai_flavor.rex: Sixteen minutes of unbroken transmission from an unverified office, asking about cargo. REX has logged it as an interrogation and is preparing a statement.
ai_flavor.chip: Every minute of this call is billable at InterPlan™ long-distance rates, both directions! CHIP has started the meter on the silences as well!
ai_flavor.ajoy: One question at a time is slow, and it gets you the corrected approach. A long speech is quick, as long as you don't promise anything in it. AJOY has heard your long speeches.

body:
From this far out, a radio message to the colony takes nine minutes to arrive and the reply nine more, so the landing office has given up on conversation. Its officer speaks for a quarter of an hour without stopping, and covers everything you might say back.

"If you said yes, thank you. If you said no, please skip to the next part. If you asked about water, I am coming to that."

They need your manifest, the crop's quarantine status and a landing slot.

choices.text: Answer one question at a time

outcome.narrative: You answer each question and wait for the next. A round takes eighteen minutes, and the rounds go on for four days, in which everyone aboard learns to make tea in exactly eighteen minutes. At the end you have a decent slot and a corrected approach that will save five of fuel.

You talk for forty minutes and cover everything, including a question you invent about whether you would give way to freighters, to which you say yes, generously. The office is delighted, as hardly anyone offers. Your approach moves to the back of the queue behind three freighters, and holding there costs three of fuel. It was, everyone agrees, a very good speech.

You start answering while their speech is still on its way, so your answers cross theirs somewhere in the dark, each one replying to something the other side has not heard yet. After an hour the office sends a short message asking if everything aboard is all right. It takes two days and two of fuel on a holding pattern to straighten out.

{crew.botanist} takes the quarantine questions and answers them in one unbroken speech about the bay. The colony's own agronomist replies the same way. For two days the two of them trade lectures across nine light-minutes while everyone else hides in the galley. The crop is cleared, and the advice that comes back with the clearance does it real good.

science_link.text: Radio between Earth and Mars takes about four to twenty-four minutes each way, depending on where the two planets are in their orbits.
science_link.label: Speed of light

title: Underarm

ai_flavor.aria: The crates are in ORBIT! They're little moons now! ARIA is so proud of them!
ai_flavor.marv: Escape velocity here is a little over eleven meters a second, which is a fast bicycle. Two crates in one orbit drift apart slowly, and then less slowly. Going after them now costs less than going later.
ai_flavor.rex: Projectiles leaving the station above escape velocity. REX wants to know who trained the thrower, and whether they are available for hire.
ai_flavor.chip: Your crates have been upgraded to Orbital Delivery! The upgrade fee is pending! Recovery is a separate line item!
ai_flavor.ajoy: Two crates in one orbit drift apart slowly, then less slowly, so the chase gets dearer by the hour. AJOY is already plotting the intercept.

body:
Phobos is twenty-odd kilometers of rubble going round Mars faster than Mars turns, and its gravity barely counts. Anything moving faster than about eleven meters a second leaves for good. Dockhands here roll things.

The new one throws. Two of your three supply crates have just cleared the dock rail, the depot and the moon, and are in orbit around Mars, close by and slowly drifting apart. The third is on the rail beside them. They are looking at it.

outcome.narrative: You cast off and go after them. Two crates in a shared orbit drift apart slowly enough to catch, and you net the first in an hour and the second a day later, with Phobos going round below you all the while. Five of fuel and two days, and both crates are back on the dock with your water and food inside them.

choices.text: Wait for the depot tug: 10 gold

outcome.narrative: The depot tug is out on another job. It comes back four days later with both crates netted to its nose, and the depot adds the tow to your bill with an apology in very small print. The new dockhand helps unload, and rolls everything.

The depot agrees it was their dock and their throw, and pays you back in the one thing Phobos has plenty of. Two sacks of ground moon go in the hold. Your water and food carry on round Mars, and will for some time. The third crate comes over very carefully, at walking pace.

science_link.text: Phobos's escape velocity is about 11 meters a second. It circles Mars in under eight hours, closer to its planet than any other known moon.
science_link.label: Phobos (moon)

title: From Behind

ai_flavor.aria: It's a dust shower, just for the ship! ARIA thinks the stern is getting a lovely polish!
ai_flavor.marv: Every hit is on the stern, so the dust is overtaking the ship. The thick plates are on the bow, pointed the wrong way. MARV would turn round, and resents how obvious that is.
ai_flavor.rex: Contact from the rear, sustained, no visible source. REX has turned every camera aft. They show nothing. REX finds that worse.
ai_flavor.chip: Your hull warranty covers frontal impacts only! Rear-end collisions go to the other party's insurer! The other party is Mars! CHIP is drafting a letter!
ai_flavor.ajoy: Every hit is on the stern, and the thick plates are on the bow. Yesterday would have been the time to turn, for the record.

body:
Something has been ticking on the hull for a day, all of it on the stern plates, steady as rain on a roof. It is dust, finer than flour, and by the way it hits it is overtaking you.

There is more ahead. Out here in the long middle of the Mars run, the old charts mark a lane where the dust runs thick, and the old charts say it comes from Mars.

choices.text: Turn round and take it on the bow

outcome.narrative: You flip the ship end for end and coast on backward, so the grit meets the plates built to meet things. The turn and the turn back cost five of fuel, and the bow gives up three points of hull and all of its paint. The stern stops ticking. The bow starts.

choices.sub: Hold through the thick of it

briefing.aria: We just hold on through the thick bits and breathe in between! Like a hug! A long, gritty hug! ARIA believes in the stern!
briefing.marv: The dust comes in surges as the lane thickens. Hold the brace through each one and vent between, or the heat takes the shield. It is all coming from behind, which is the side the ship was not built for.
briefing.rex: Rear contact, rising density. Brace on every surge, vent between. No cover in any direction. REX would like the record to show he hates being followed.
briefing.chip: SternGuard™ Rear Deflector sold separately, and not by you! Hold on the surges, release between! CHIP is legally required to add: good luck!
briefing.ajoy: Hold on each surge and let go in between, or the heat builds and the shield drops. You could still turn round, if anyone's asking AJOY. Nobody is, so: hold.

perfect.aria: Through the whole lane and the stern is SPARKLING! ARIA always knew it was the stern's time to shine!
perfect.marv: Every surge held. Three points of hull for the whole lane. MARV has checked the figure twice, because it is lower than he had it.
perfect.rex: Held the whole run. Contact broken off. REX will keep the aft cameras on for a while yet.
perfect.chip: Zero claims filed! Your loyalty discount on SternGuard™ has been noted and will be offered at full price!
perfect.ajoy: You held every surge. Well done. AJOY would still have turned round, but well done.

good.aria: The stern got a little scuffed, but scuffs are just character! ARIA loves this ship's character!
good.marv: Most of the surges held. One came in on bare plate, and a radiator seam went with it. Seven of hull, and a radiator seam, as calculated.
good.rex: One surge through the brace. Hull damage, minor air loss. Acceptable for an attack from the rear.
good.chip: Partial coverage applies! Your deductible is the stern! CHIP has filed the claim with Mars, care of Mars!
good.ajoy: You let go early on one surge. It cost you a radiator seam. The orange flash comes first, as AJOY may have mentioned.

poor.aria: The shield took a little rest halfway! It's so important to rest! The stern is very well ventilated now!
poor.marv: The brace failed early. Twelve of hull, a good deal of air, and a stern that will need looking at for the rest of the voyage. MARV had a figure in mind. This is it.
poor.rex: Brace lost under sustained rear fire. Hull breached aft. REX recommends never coming this way again.
poor.chip: Coverage voided by early release! Mars has declined liability! CHIP has never seen Mars decline anything so fast!
poor.ajoy: You let go too soon, and the lane did the rest. Turning round was the five-fuel option, for next time.

outcome.narrative: You hold the course through the thick of the lane.

perfect.narrative: You hold the course through two days of the thick of the lane and keep the brace up on every surge. Two of fuel and three of hull, and the stern comes out the far side scoured to bare metal and in one piece.

good.narrative: Two days in the thick of the lane, and one surge catches the brace down. Seven of hull, two of fuel, and {cost.o2} of air through a radiator seam that has to be found by listening for it.

poor.narrative: The brace goes down early, and for most of two days the stern takes the lane bare. Twelve of hull, {cost.o2} of air, two of fuel. Every bunk aft has to be moved forward, and the aft bunks stay empty for the rest of the voyage.

choices.text: Cut the drive and let it pass

outcome.narrative: You cut the drive and let the dust overtake you. The ticking thins day by day, and on the eighth it stops. The wait costs {cost.water} units of water and {cost.food} of food, and the stern two points of hull for the first days, while it was still thick.

You fly on and let it tick. By the far edge of the lane it has worn the stern plates to a dull shine, nine points of hull, and opened a radiator seam that leaks {cost.o2} points of air before anyone finds it. It was only dust. It was a great deal of only dust.

science_link.text: In 2021, dust hits on the backs of the Juno probe's solar panels, counted between Earth and the asteroid belt, suggested that the dust behind the zodiacal light comes from Mars.
science_link.label: Juno (spacecraft)

title: Don't Say It

ai_flavor.aria: ARIA has been asked not to say how well the crop is doing! It is doing SO well! ARIA has not said a single thing!
ai_flavor.marv: Plants that are handled grow short and stout. MARV has counted the handling. This crop is the most patted object aboard by a margin he declines to state, out of respect for the streak.
ai_flavor.rex: Every hand aboard has made unauthorized contact with the crop, repeatedly. REX can find no hostile intent in any of it. He finds that more suspicious, not less.
ai_flavor.chip: CHIP's lawyers advise against jinxing a protected asset! LuckGuard covers the crop against praise! Premiums are due whether anyone talks or not!
ai_flavor.ajoy: The touching is what's slowing it down. Stop it and the crop catches up, and the crew sulks. Keep it and the crop comes in short. AJOY noticed the stems a week ago and was told not to jinx it.

body:
Three good weeks running in the growbay, and not one word said about the {crop.name}. The crew agreed, without a meeting, that praise would end the streak.

Instead they touch it for luck: a leaf between finger and thumb on the way to the galley, a pat on the way back. Every stem in the bay has been handled hundreds of times.

The growth log has noticed. The stems are coming in short and thick, and the whole bay is running behind.

choices.text: Say it out loud at dinner

outcome.narrative: At dinner you say that the crop is doing well. A fork goes down. Then nothing happens, all evening, and that is worse. The luck is plainly spent, so the touching stops, and within the week the new growth is running long and green and back on schedule. You are treated as someone who got away with something.

You leave the luck where it is. The crop goes on coming up short and stout and late, so sturdy that a dropped tray bounces off a row without bending a stem. Every hand aboard pats it on the way past. The streak is never mentioned, and holds.

choices.text: Pot one plant by the hatch for luck

outcome.narrative: You lift one plant into a pot and stand it beside the hatch, where there is no getting past without touching it. The rest of the bay is left alone and catches up. The plant by the hatch grows no taller than a fist and as thick as a thumb, and is the most loved thing aboard.

science_link.text: Plants that are touched, shaken or blown about grow shorter and stockier than sheltered ones. Repeated handling holds back their upward growth and thickens the stem.
science_link.label: Thigmomorphogenesis

title: Two Shares

ai_flavor.aria: The crew wrote a whole CONSTITUTION! ARIA is so proud! ARIA would like a share! ARIA would spend it on hats!
